A metodologia consistiu em uma revisão de literatura de caráter qualitativo e exploratório, fundamentada em bases de dados científicas. Os resultados evidenciam que a prática regular de exercícios no ambiente de trabalho reduz significativamente a incidência de Distúrbios Osteomusculares Relacionados ao Trabalho (DORT) e Lesões por Esforços Repetitivos (LER). Além dos benefícios fisiológicos, como a melhora da circulação sanguínea e da flexibilidade, a intervenção atua positivamente na saúde mental, reduzindo os níveis de estresse e ansiedade cotidianos. Para as organizações, os impactos traduzem-se na diminuição do absenteísmo, na redução de custos com assistência médica e no aumento direto da produtividade, impulsionado pelo incremento da motivação e do clima organizacional. Conclui-se que a ginástica laboral é uma ferramenta estratégica indispensável para o desenvolvimento de ambientes de trabalho sustentáveis e saudáveis, justificando investimentos contínuos em programas de qualidade de vida voltados ao trabalhador. Palavras-chave: Ginástica Laboral. Saúde Ocupacional. Ergonomia. THE BENEFITS OF WORKPLACE EXERCISES FOR WORKER HEALTH AND PRODUCTIVITY ABSTRACT Workplace gymnastics stands out as an important ergonomic intervention in the corporate environment, focusing on health promotion and the prevention of occupational diseases. The objective of this theoretical study was to analyze the physical, psychological, and organizational benefits of workplace gymnastics for both workers and companies. The methodology consisted of a qualitative and exploratory literature review, based on scientific databases. The results show that the regular practice of exercises in the workplace significantly reduces the incidence of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WRMD). In addition to physiological benefits, such as improved blood circulation and flexibility, the intervention positively affects mental health, reducing daily stress and anxiety levels. For organizations, the impacts translate into decreased absenteeism, reduced medical care costs, and a direct increase in productivity, driven by increased motivation and organizational climate. It is concluded that workplace gymnastics is an indispensable strategic tool for the development of sustainable and healthy work environments, justifying continuous investments in quality of life programs for workers. Keywords: Workplace Gymnastics. Occupational Health. Ergonomics. LOS BENEFICIOS DE LA GIMNASIA EN EL LUGAR DE TRABAJO PARA LA SALUD Y LA PRODUCTIVIDAD DE LOS TRABAJADORES RESUMEN La gimnasia en el lugar de trabajo se destaca como una importante intervención ergonómica en el entorno corporativo, enfocada en promover la salud y prevenir lesiones laborales. El objetivo de este estudio teórico fue analizar los beneficios físicos, psicológicos y organizacionales de la gimnasia en el lugar de trabajo para los trabajadores y las empresas. La metodología consistió en una revisión cualitativa y exploratoria de la literatura, basada en bases de datos científicas. Los resultados muestran que la práctica regular de ejercicios en el lugar de trabajo reduce significativamente la incidencia de trastornos musculoesqueléticos relacionados con el trabajo (TMRT) y lesiones por esfuerzo repetitivo (LER). Además de los beneficios fisiológicos, como la mejora de la circulación sanguínea y la flexibilidad, la intervención tiene un impacto positivo en la salud mental, reduciendo los niveles diarios de estrés y ansiedad. Para las organizaciones, los impactos se traducen en una disminución del absentismo, una reducción de los costos de atención médica y un aumento directo de la productividad, impulsado por una mayor motivación y un mejor clima organizacional. Se concluye que la gimnasia en el lugar de trabajo es una herramienta estratégica indispensable para el desarrollo de entornos laborales sostenibles y saludables, lo que justifica la inversión continua en programas de calidad de vida dirigidos a los trabajadores. Palabras clave: Gimnasia en el lugar de trabajo. Salud ocupacional. Ergonomía.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator $κ$ of 0.82-1.00. We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

Crime-related social media content provides valuable information for situational awareness and policy support; however, engagement-driven signals, such as likes and retweets, can introduce popularity bias and affect predictive outcomes. This study proposes a fairness-aware, Pareto-based, multi-objective optimization framework for feature selection and Random Forest hyperparameter optimization, leveraging textual and engagement features. A dataset of 32,000 crime-related tweets covering Fraud, Accident, and Murder was represented using TF-IDF and interaction-based features. Four optimization strategies, Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL), and Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), were comparatively evaluated. NSGA-II jointly maximized classification performance while minimizing a fairness penalty based on Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), and Equality of Opportunity Difference (EOD). In this study, fairness refers to mitigating engagement-driven popularity bias across behavioral user groups rather than demographic discrimination. NSGA-II achieved an accuracy of 0.8118 and an F1-score of 0.8051, with an SPD of 0.08, DI of 0.97, and EOD of 0.06, demonstrating the most favorable balance between predictive performance and behavioral fairness. Although removing engagement features improved standalone Accuracy and F1-score, retaining them enabled explicit assessment and mitigation of engagement-driven bias. Stratified cross-validation and comparative analysis across the optimization strategies further supported the consistency of the observed results. The findings demonstrate that integrating fairness objectives directly into Pareto-based optimization provides a practical and interpretable approach to balancing predictive effectiveness and engagement-driven fairness in crime-related social media analytics.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and beginning of a decentralized platform offers the possibility to replace the welfare model of career mobility for underserved populations and next generation workforce. The focus of this study is to analyze the contribution of Pathfinder AI, an AI aimed decentralized platform designed to resolve the barriers marginalized workers face when it comes to gaining career advancement opportunities. Taking a hold of AI tools and block chain technologies Pathfinder AI intends to eliminate the barriers to job opportunity access democratizing access to job opportunities, personalize career development pathway and knock down systemic biases in recruitment process. The study tests this relationship between the usage of AI tools, career mobility, as well as job search success with a survey-based methodology involving 400 participants from various backgrounds. An analysis is done by using SPSS to conduct descriptive statistics, regression analysis, as well as Chi-square tests to evaluate how Pathfinder AI can enhance career outcomes for underserved workers. Results indicate that the more AI tools an employee utilizes, the greater likelihood they have of a change in career mobility (B = 0.56, p < 0.001) and success in job search (r = 0.47, p < 0.01). Participants using Pathfinder AI also saw a 15% boost over Those not using the Platform when using the Platform offering. The results indicate that Pathfinder AI holds a very large positive effect on career mobility for employees for whom fewer traditional career advancement resources are available. It is decentralized that it creates a greater level of transparency, trust and fair job matching for the marginalized groups. The final point of this study is that AI driven decentralized platform can change the future of work and allow all workers to have equal access to career growth and economic mobility irrespective of the background they come from.

documents.abstract: Early and accurate detection of pea diseases is essential for reducing crop losses and supporting precision agriculture. Although deep learning methods have shown good performance in plant disease classification, CNN-based models may have limitations in learning long-range relationships and detailed disease features. In this study, an explainable transformer-based framework, named PEAS-DeiT, is proposed for automated pea leaf disease classification. The proposed approach integrates a multi-scale spatial attention mechanism into the Data-efficient Image Transformer (DeiT) architecture to enhance the representation of disease-related visual features. A unified pea leaf disease dataset (UPLDD) was constructed by combining multiple publicly available datasets, covering six classes, including five disease categories and healthy samples. The proposed model was evaluated against CNN-based and transformer-based architectures using five-fold cross-validation. Furthermore, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) analysis was performed to investigate the regions contributing to model predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that PEAS-DeiT achieved an accuracy of 93.11%, showing competitive performance compared with the evaluated CNN and transformer-based models. The gradient-based saliency analysis also revealed localized response patterns in several evaluated samples, providing qualitative insight into the image regions contributing to model predictions. Statistical analyses were conducted to evaluate the performance differences among the compared models. These findings indicate that PEAS-DeiT provides a competitive approach for pea leaf disease classification within the evaluated experimental setting.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: In Intelligent Transport Systems, protecting vulnerable road users, specifically pedestrians, is a paramount challenge. The present work contributes to this field, putting forth a distributed architecture in which vehicles connected to the cellular infrastructure collect pedestrians' trajectories and fine-tune a foundation model for pedestrian trajectory forecasting via federated training. A server positioned at the edge of the cellular network is responsible for aggregating the local model's parameters from the vehicles and updating the global model's parameters. To reduce radio resource utilization, Low-Rank Adaptation is proposed; to decrease both the number and the size of updates, an increase in the number of training rounds performed by the vehicles per communication round is put forth. A novel figure of merit is then introduced to quantify the use of radio resources dedicated to Vehicle-to-Infrastructure communications as required by the federated solution. The proposed scheme delivers excellent prediction accuracy while significantly reducing the communication cost compared to alternative federated training methods. This shows that combining fine-tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation, and a reduction of the communication periodicity between the vehicles and the edge server is key to enabling a distributed approach to trajectory prediction in vehicular environments.

Micro, small, and medium enterprises require practical digital marketing skills to produce attractive and consistent promotional content. This program aimed to strengthen the digital marketing capacity of 30 food and beverage MSMEs in Bojongloa Kaler District, Bandung City, through Generative Artificial Intelligence-based training and mentoring. Activities were implemented through needs identification, material and instrument preparation, interactive training, guided practice, mentoring, evaluation, and follow-up support. The training covered an introduction to GenAI, prompt engineering, caption writing, product descriptions, content ideas, promotional calendars, and simple digital design. Evaluation results showed that participants' average understanding increased from 54.2% in the pre-test to 96.4% in the post-test, representing a 42.2 percentage-point improvement. Participants produced reusable outputs, including captions, product descriptions, prompt templates, content calendars, and digital promotional materials. Although long-term sales and social media performance were not measured, these outputs provide a foundation for future monitoring and independent content production.

The decline in student learning interest in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) at Madrasah Ibtidaiyah (MI) remains a pedagogical challenge, particularly in regions constrained by limited digital infrastructure and dominant conventional lecturing methods. This study aims to examine the effectiveness of Wordwall as an interactive learning medium in enhancing students’ learning interest. A quasi-experimental design with a pretest-posttest control group was employed. The sample consisted of 64 fourth-grade MI students in Muara Bungo Regency, cluster-randomly assigned into experimental (n=32) and control (n=32) groups. The main instrument was a learning interest questionnaire adapted from Keller’s ARCS theory, validated with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.887. Data were analyzed using paired and independent sample t-tests, N-Gain, and Cohen’s d effect size. Results indicated a significant increase in learning interest in the experimental class (p = 0.001; N-Gain = 0.64; d = 0.91), while the control class showed no meaningful change. Qualitative findings from observations and teacher interviews confirmed that gamification elements, instant feedback, and Islamic contextual visualization in Wordwall contributed to enhanced affective and cognitive engagement. This study provides empirical contributions for integrating educational technology into PAI instruction at madrasahs and offers a practical model aligned with the Ministry of Religious Affairs’ madrasah digitalization policy.

The rapid growth of the digital economy has opened vast opportunities through gig economy platforms, yet high school students and teachers often lack the digital literacy and skills needed to capitalize on these prospects productively. This community service program aimed to empower the economic potential of students and teachers at SMA IRA Medan by delivering education and technical training on digital freelance platforms integrated with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning tools. The methodology comprised three main stages: pre-implementation (need analysis, module synthesis, and institutional coordination), implementation (interactive seminar, live demonstration of AI tools, and hands-on portfolio creation workshops), and evaluation (pre-test/post-test analysis and mentoring). The activity took place at SMA IRA Medan on September 30, 2026, involving 40 participants consisting of students and teachers. The results demonstrated a significant increase in participant understanding, rising from an average of 23.1% in the pre-test to 88.8% in the post-test, an increase of 65.7%. Furthermore, 87.5% of participants successfully created active profiles and digital portfolios on platforms such as Sribulancer and Projects.co.id. This initiative successfully fostered a digital entrepreneurship mindset, equipping students and teachers with monetizable skills to support sustainable economic independence.

The rapid development of digital technology requires young people to utilize technology creatively and productively. This community service program aimed to strengthen students’ digital literacy through an introduction to information technology, Canva training, and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) at Pesantren Madani Sungai Alam. The program involved 20 students and was conducted on August 18 and 20, 2026, using a practice-based training approach consisting of material presentation, demonstration, hands-on practice, work appreciation, and mentoring. Program evaluation was carried out descriptively through direct observation and assessment of participants' practical work. The results demonstrated that participants gained practical experience in utilizing technology, Canva, and AI tools to develop creative ideas and produce digital content. This program establishes a foundational skill set that can be further enhanced through sustainable mentoring.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into the workplace, the risk that occupations will be replaced by AI has received widespread attention. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms linking AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception to individual withdrawal behaviors remain underexplored. Taking identity threat as an explanatory lens, this study integrates Identity Threat Theory (ITT) and Technology Threat Avoidance Theory (TTAT) to investigate the effect of occupational replacement risk perception on employee withdrawal behavior, with professional identity, work meaningfulness, and job insecurity serving as mediators and technological self-efficacy as a moderator. Two studies were conducted to test the theoretical model developed in this research. Study 1 developed and validated the AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception scale. Study 2 employed a three-wave time-lagged survey design to test the hypotheses. The results show that occupational replacement risk perception is positively associated with withdrawal behavior through decreased professional identity and work meaningfulness as well as increased job insecurity. Furthermore, these indirect effects are weaker among employees with higher technological self-efficacy. By illuminating the identity-threat mechanism that links AI-induced occupational replacement risk perception to employee behavior, this study opens the black box of how AI shapes employee responses, and it concludes with a discussion of the theoretical contributions and practical implications of these findings.

Abstract The widespread adoption of large language models has increased the need to distinguish human-authored text from AI-generated content, including cases in which generated text is subsequently rewritten or paraphrased. In practice, many detectors output only a single AI-likelihood score or percentage, offering limited transparency and little indication of whether a passage appears directly AI-written (AIW) or AI-rewritten (AIR). This study presents an agentic detection framework for two connected tasks: binary provenance detection (Human versus AI) and conditional subtype detection (AIW versus AIR). The dataset combined the Human-ChatGPT Comparison Corpus (HC3) and the ai-text-detection-pile with 4,348 pre-generated AIR records produced by a single GPT-based rewriting workflow. The proposed Qwen–LangGraph AI agent was compared to a HashingVectorizer–TF-IDF–SGD classifier, DeBERTa-v3-xsmall, and ELECTRA-small. On the binary test set, DeBERTa-v3-xsmall achieved the best discrimination (99.4995% accuracy and 99.9911% AUROC), whereas the agent achieved 98.8816% accuracy and 99.9187% AUROC. On the AI-only test set (10,769 AIW; 1,274 AIR), the agent obtained the highest threshold-based accuracy (96.7367%), macro-F1 (90.0357%), and AIR F1 (81.8643%), but its AUROC (83.2507%) and AUPR (79.7336%) were lower than those of the DeBERTa-v3-xsmall and ELECTRA-small transformers. Paired DeLong and McNemar analyses with Holm correction showed that the agent improved threshold-based AIR performance over the lexical baseline. Interpretability was operationalised through lexical weights, linguistic and out-of-distribution diagnostics, sentence-level indicators, and route traces. The findings support the use of AI as decision support, not as automated proof of plagiarism or misconduct.

Large language model (LLM) evaluators are increasingly used to assess personalized assistants, yet whether they can reliably judge personalization has rarely been tested. We introduce PersEvalBench, a benchmark testing whether an evaluator can recognize appropriate and inappropriate uses of user history. It contains 403 multi-episode scenarios where user information should persist, transfer, or cease to apply. The benchmark covers nine controlled error subtypes across three families: under-personalization, over-personalization, and misapplied-state errors. Human audits confirm that generated errors match their intended types and that the prescribed uses of user information are reasonable. Across five LLM evaluators, recognition of controlled personalization errors remains limited even with the full dialogue history. On the human-evaluated subset, under-personalization shows the largest gap: humans recognize 94.4% of these errors, compared with 63.9% for the strongest reported evaluator. Evaluators often recognize that a response is problematic but reverse the error direction, mistaking failure to follow an applicable preference (UNDER) for use of an inapplicable preference (OVER). Easier evidence access offers little help: highlighting the relevant history turns raises error recognition only slightly, suggesting that the remaining difficulty lies in judging what role that information should play in the response.

documents.abstract: (1) Background: The aim of this study was to analyze how teacher trainees and teachers relate to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education across socio-emotional, attitudinal, competency-based, and ethical dimensions, considering the influence of personal, academic, and professional variables. The study was conceptually framed by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), complemented by DigCompEdu as a broader reference for teacher digital competence. (2) Methods: A quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive, cross-sectional design was developed with a sample of 1292 participants from Andalusia, consisting mainly of university students, along with teachers. The ACISE-IA scale, consisting of 39 items developed by Serrano-García et al. (2026), was used for data collection. (3) Results: The results showed that age and teaching experience are negatively associated with favorable attitudes and digital competence, while academic performance is positively related to greater openness, critical reflection, and perception of competence. Likewise, significant differences were identified according to the branch of knowledge, employment status, and academic year, with more positive assessments among students and in social science areas. (4) Conclusions: Overall, the findings show that the relationship with AI is not homogeneous, but rather modulated by educational and professional trajectories, underscoring the need to design flexible teacher training models that integrate technological development with pedagogical, emotional, and ethical reflection. These findings also contribute to educational sustainability by highlighting the importance of developing teacher training strategies that support the responsible and sustained integration of AI into educational systems.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare by enabling integration of genomic sequencing, wearable sensor streams, electronic health records, and environmental exposure data into predictive and preventive clinical systems. These advances support a transition from reactive treatment toward individualized precision health while simultaneously strengthening population-level analytics and public health decision making. Polygenic risk modeling, pharmacogenomics, real-world evidence platforms, and learning health systems illustrate how multimodal biomedical data infrastructures can improve early detection, treatment selection, and disease forecasting. However, these innovations introduce challenges involving algorithmic bias, privacy governance, interoperability, and equitable access to emerging technologies. Responsible deployment of large-scale health data requires transparency, regulatory oversight, and inclusive datasets that reflect diverse populations. The future of medicine will depend on balancing personalization with fairness while ensuring that AI-driven healthcare improves outcomes not only for individuals but also for entire communities through precision public health strategies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract—Physical Artificial Intelligence (Physical AI) represents a transformative frontier in autonomous cyber-physical robotics, shifting machine intelligence from disembodied algorithmic computation into dynamical systems that perceive, reason, and actuate directly within the physical world. While pure reinforcement learning (RL) and kinematic motion planners excel in controlled, isolated environments, deploying high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) bipedal humanoids and dexterous anthropomorphic hands in real-world unstructured settings introduces severe physical and computational bottlenecks: non-smooth contact mechanics, extreme sim-to-real transfer gaps, high-dimensional non-convex hybrid dynamics, and closed-loop motor bandwidth constraints. Differentiable Physics engines—which compute exact analytical state and contact gradients through forward simulation—alongside massively parallel GPU-accelerated domain randomization, establish a foundational computational methodology to bridge this chasm. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Physical AI for whole-body humanoid locomotion and dexterous tactile manipulation. We formalize the non-linear hybrid dynamical equations of underactuated bipedal contact, derive gradient backpropagation through Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) friction cones, and model domain randomization over non-stationary physical distribution manifolds. Furthermore, we construct an empirical robotic evaluation testbed comprising full-scale bipedal humanoid platforms (Unitree H1, Fourier GR-1) and high-density optical tactile arrays (GelSight Svelte) evaluated across 800 challenging trials spanning uneven terrain locomotion, dynamic external impulse rejection, and blind in-hand object re-orientation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that differentiable physics-guided policy search achieves an 88.6% zero-shot sim-to-real locomotion transfer success rate, reducing training sample complexity by 4.2x over model-free PPO while bounding tracking error under 120 N external lateral impulses. Concurrently, high-frequency optical tactile feedback raises blind in-hand manipulation success by 54.2% over vision-only baselines. Finally, we formulate open challenges in non-rigid soft body contact differentiability, whole-body tactile-semantic foundation models, and real-time safety barrier certificates. Index Terms—Physical AI, Differentiable Physics, Sim-to-Real Transfer, Humanoid Locomotion, Whole-Body Control (WBC), Tactile Manipulation, Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP), Domain Randomization.

Abstract. Data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are increasingly positioned as alternatives or complements to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, yet systematic model evaluation studies that compare both paradigms under controlled experimental conditions remain limited. Here we present a structured model evaluation framework applying standardised verification metrics to assess a regional WRF configuration against three publicly available AI models – GraphCast, AIFS Single 1.0, and FuXi – over three high-impact flood events in Luxembourg and the Greater Region (2016, 2018, and 2021), comprising 90 simulation days and over 7300 matched forecast-observation pairs. The WRF model employs a three-dimensional variational (3D-VAR) data assimilation scheme ingesting GNSS Zenith Total Delay and conventional observations on a 6-hourly Rapid Update Cycle. All systems are initialised from ERA5 reanalysis to ensure consistent initial conditions. Categorical precipitation scores at the 1 mm threshold and continuous temperature metrics at surface stations serve as verification targets. Data assimilation measurably improves WRF's categorical precipitation skill (Critical Success Index: 0.306 to 0.341) while leaving near-surface temperature largely unchanged, demonstrating the value of the assimilation scheme. AIFS achieves the highest detection rate (POD 0.765) and net categorical skill (CSI 0.370), GraphCast and AIFS reduce temperature RMSE by ~10 % relative to assimilated WRF, and WRF alone reproduces the observed mesoscale precipitation structure of the catastrophic July 2021 flood. The per-event breakdown reveals no skill degradation for AI models on out-of-sample events, suggesting that meteorological regime rather than training-data overlap governs model performance. These results provide a replicable model evaluation methodology for benchmarking emerging data-driven NWP systems against observation-corrected regional models.

Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on ToolBench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross-category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt-oss-120b). We characterize a stub-hallucination failure mode (the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names) that acts as a double-edged sword: on simple queries PtR's stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, yet on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs. We further analyze token overhead and show that PtR's extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction, one that can be driven by a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtP's top-1 retrieval score).

The Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO) benchmark standardized evaluation in molecular optimization, but it is built on simple property-based oracles that do not capture structure-based drug design. As the field has moved to docking-based objectives, evaluation practice has become unstandardized, and different methods report results on different docking tasks, often without a shared protocol for fair comparison or sample-efficiency constraints. To address this, we introduce Practical Molecular Optimization for Docking (PMO-Dock), a benchmark and protocol for docking-based optimization consisting of 25 tasks covering hit generation, lead optimization, and a new specificity task requiring strong on-target binding while penalizing off-target interactions. The protocol separates model development from final evaluation: validation tasks are used for hyperparameter tuning, and test tasks are held out for final evaluation and are not used during development. Evaluation on the test tasks is done under a strict oracle budget to reflect realistic drug-discovery settings. We benchmark four diverse high-performing methods spanning different optimization paradigms, Saturn (reinforcement learning), GenMol (discrete diffusion), Genetic-guided GFlowNet, and ChemLlama (LLM-based evolutionary search). Our results show no universally best method across tasks, additional analyses of hyperparameter transfer (cross-task and cross-category) and sensitivity show that transfer is often limited and varies by method, motivating method-dependent selection strategies. This benchmark provides a concrete standard for evaluating generalization to unseen tasks and sample efficiency under a limited test-time oracle budget.

documents.abstract: Objective: To map how exercise and physical-education research with university students has implemented assessment, subgroup targeting, individualized prescription, monitoring, feedback, and response-based adjustment, and to identify what is still required for a reproducible closed-loop precision-support system. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews. PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL Ultimate were searched on August 21, 2026, for English-language studies, supplemented by an existing 28-report full-text seed set. Eligible studies involved university students and evaluated an exercise, physical-education, fitness-testing, monitoring, or feedback component relevant to tailoring exercise support. A five-level framework was applied: standardized provision (level 0), subgroup targeting (level 1), assessment- or feedback-informed adaptation (level 2), individual prescription (level 3), and response-adaptive closed loop (level 4). Results: The searches and seed set identified 403 records; 358 unique records were screened, 48 reports were assessed in full text, and 30 studies entered the evidence map. Fifteen studies used standardized provision, three targeted a predefined subgroup, six implemented assessment, monitoring, or personalized feedback without a complete individual prescription, and six reported individual exercise prescriptions. No study fully specified a level-4 closed loop with prospective monitoring variables, decision thresholds, and reproducible rules for changing frequency, intensity, time, or type. Exercise programs improved selected fitness, body-composition, physical-activity, and mental-health outcomes, but effects were outcome-specific and heterogeneous. Wearables and mobile platforms made monitoring scalable, yet fixed goals, multicomponent designs, and limited use of monitored data for treatment decisions constrained personalization. Assessment feedback could also reduce competence and intrinsic motivation when interpreted negatively. Conclusions: The literature has progressed beyond uniform exercise delivery, but digital monitoring should not be equated with precision. A defensible university model requires an auditable chain from multidimensional assessment to stratification, FITT prescription, process monitoring, interpretable feedback, and threshold-based adjustment, alongside evaluation of safety, equity, adherence, teacher workload, and operational efficiency.

documents.abstract: Air pollution currently represents a significant environmental challenge with a direct impact on both public health and ecosystems. One of the aims of this paper is to predict the concentration of particulate matter PM10 and CO2 in the air using machine learning methods, specifically by employing various types of neural networks, including feedforward, convolutional, and recurrent models. The aim is also to compare the performance of these architectures in processing univariate time series with different temporal resolutions (monthly, hourly). The study uses real data from the Slovak Hydrometeorological Institute (SHMÚ) and modelled emissions from the EDGAR database. The models were trained, optimized, and evaluated using standard error metrics. The results showed that Conv1D models achieved the highest accuracy on hourly data of PM10, while feedforward architectures performed best on monthly national data of CO2. The findings confirm the potential of artificial intelligence methods as a tool for environmental monitoring and decision support in air quality protection. Opportunities for extending the models with meteorological variables and applying them in real-time warning systems are also discussed.

Smart electrical distribution networks are becoming more observable, automated, and data intensive, yet maintenance practice often remains dominated by periodic inspection or intervention after alarms and failures. This review develops a predictive maintenance framework that connects artificial intelligence and data analytics with the operational realities of distribution transformers, on-load tap changers, switchgear, circuit breakers, feeders, cables, substations, smart meters, and distributed-energy interfaces. The evidence base is restricted to peer-reviewed work published from 2020 to 2025 and is synthesized through a structured integrative review focused on data provenance, condition indicators, learning tasks, validation practice, interpretability, uncertainty, deployment constraints, and maintenance decision linkage. The review shows that useful predictive maintenance cannot be reduced to selecting a high-performing classifier. Reliable deployment requires a chain of asset-aware sensing, data-quality control, representation learning, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, health forecasting, uncertainty estimation, consequence assessment, and human-governed maintenance orchestration. Deep learning and ensemble methods improve representation of nonlinear and temporal degradation, while digital twins can provide synchronized context, scenario testing, and traceability; however, scarce fault labels, changing operating regimes, class imbalance, fragmented semantics, cyber risk, and weak external validation remain major obstacles. A layered framework is therefore proposed in which analytical outputs are converted into risk-calibrated maintenance actions rather than isolated predictions. The framework emphasizes evidence quality, cross-asset generalization, explainable reasoning, model monitoring, and feedback from completed work orders. It provides a research and implementation architecture for moving smart distribution maintenance from condition visibility toward dependable, auditable, and economically meaningful predictive decision support.

Attrition among employees is one of the greatest concerns in the modern organization due to high expenses caused by recruiting new personnel, productivity losses, and reduction of corporate knowledge. In the research under consideration, there is a developed predictive modeling system intended to predict employee attrition and develop appropriate retention strategies. The proposed methodology uses complex machine learning techniques such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and ensembles along with mechanisms of explainable artificial intelligence that provide transparency of the model and facilitate its application. By applying the IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition dataset containing information about employees' features, the framework uses advanced techniques of preprocessing, class balancing, and feature engineering to take into account complex aspects of attrition. As a result of experiments, it is revealed that the ensemble model demonstrates better forecasting results compared to baseline models. The interpretation of results based on the SHAP technique shows that overtime, monthly income, length of service, and job satisfaction are the most important factors affecting attrition. Thus, the research provides an innovative approach that will help turn human resource management into proactive workforce planning.

Current artificial intelligence (AI) methods for power electronics converters make limited use of the abundant unlabeled data generated during real-world operation. This underexplored resource holds significant potential for advancing model performance. To address this gap, this paper presents PE-TSFM, a time-series foundation model tailored for power module health monitoring. The model adopts the PatchTST architecture combined with self-supervised learning and is trained on more than 143 million timestamps, where over 98\% of this training data is unlabeled and collected directly from an operating traction converter. In degradation classification tasks, PE-TSFM achieves an accuracy of 87\%, considerably surpassing five conventional time-series AI models whose performance ranges from 27\% to 45\%. These results demonstrate the model's strong few-shot learning capability and generalization across different operating conditions. This work promotes a shift from narrowly focused models in power electronics toward unified, scalable foundation models that can unlock value from large-scale unlabeled operational data.

The presence of a human reviewer in an AI-mediated decision does not establish that the person could inspect the relevant evidence, reconsider a preconfigured set of alternatives, or legitimately change the course of action. This is not a novel discovery: research in human factors, meaningful human control, signal detection, and human–AI interaction already identifies relevant components. This paper treats Preservation of Effective Judgment (PEJ) as a bounded, falsifiable research problem rather than a validated psychological construct or a proprietary assessment score. It asks whether a state-sensitive reconstruction that distinguishes (i) available epistemic and procedural opportunities, (ii) observable examination and reconsideration, and (iii) feasible interventions and verified material effects produces more informative claims than established comparator frameworks. The contribution is a proposed comparison logic, a public observational grammar, explicit rival explanations, and designs capable of returning null, redundant, or adverse findings. It does not assert construct originality, report human-subject results, establish legal compliance, or validate a diagnostic instrument. Related behavioral-assurance proposals from Behavieural are credited as independent prior work. A failure to demonstrate incremental explanatory or reconstructive value would justify narrowing PEJ to a documentary synthesis or retiring it as a separate construct. Version 1.0 includes a substantive comparison with Daria Lepikhina (2026), section 3.1 and reference [19]. Conceptual and methodological working paper; not peer reviewed. 11 pages, 19 references. English text with a Spanish abstract.

documents.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies (1 January 2020 to 23 September 2026) that develop or evaluate pretrained foundation models (DNA and RNA language models, single-cell foundation models, multimodal epigenomic models) for gene-regulatory prediction tasks. The review maps the evidence and pools within-study comparisons in which a foundation model and a task-specific deep-learning model trained from scratch are evaluated on the same test data. Reported according to PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S. The full protocol (amendment v0.3, 12 October 2026) is attached to this registration.

OBJECTIVES: Silent vertebral fractures are common but under-recognised. We aimed to estimate the prevalence in an asymptomatic population and to identify demographic and clinical predictors using the UK Biobank data. MATERIALS AND METHODS: DXA spine images from 2446 asymptomatic UK Biobank participants aged 40-79 years were analysed retrospectively. Vertebral fractures were defined as moderate or severe deformities (≥ 25% vertebral height loss). Fractures were identified using an artificial-intelligence-assisted six-point morphometric algorithm with manual correction and radiologist confirmation. Associations with age, sex, bone mineral density (BMD), body mass index (BMI), medication, and back pain were analysed. RESULTS: A total of 2446 participants (mean age 62.0 ± 7.4 years; 1151 men) were analysed. Moderate or severe vertebral fractures were identified in 356 participants (14.6%). Prevalence increased with age, from 9.4% in participants aged 40-49 years to 19.6% in those aged 70-79 years. Fractures were more common in men than women (18.8% vs. 10.8%; adjusted OR 0.51 for women vs. men, 95% CI 0.40-0.66; p < 0.001). BMD and most conventional clinical risk factors had limited predictive value. CONCLUSIONS: Silent vertebral fractures are common in midlife, frequently occur in individuals with normal bone density, and are more prevalent in men. Conventional clinical risk factors have a limited ability to identify affected individuals. KEY POINTS: Question Silent vertebral fractures are frequently overlooked in asymptomatic individuals, and their prevalence and demographic distribution in middle-aged adults are not well-characterised. Findings In a large asymptomatic cohort, vertebral fractures were common, showed male predominance, and were frequently present in individuals without low bone mineral density or recognised clinical risk factors. Clinical relevance Silent vertebral fractures are prevalent in asymptomatic adults and are poorly captured by conventional risk assessment, indicating limitations of current approaches to fracture identification.

This study examines the impact of integrating artificial intelligence tools on the principle of good administration, enshrined in Article 41 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, focusing on the guarantee of a reasonable time for resolving administrative requests. The paper begins with the legal and case-law foundation of the reasonable time standard, both at European level (ECtHR and CJEU case law) and at national level (Romanian court practice and the express regulation of time limits in Romanian legislation), before analysing, in a second stage, the positive contributions that digitalisation may bring to compliance with this standard: faster processing of standardised requests, reduction of human error, increased transparency and accountability, easier access to public information, and optimisation of complex procedures. The study also identifies the structural limits of this positive impact and the autonomous risks generated by the use of AI – technological dependency, algorithmic errors, excessive standardisation, algorithmic opacity, diluted accountability and unequal access to performant digital resources. The central conclusion is that, in the age of artificial intelligence, the reasonable time standard becomes a dynamic standard, whose observance depends on a set of institutional and technological safeguards.

documents.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity model motivates representing these responses as a surrogate Jacobian. Ridge regression on human labels learns a correction to the baseline score. The resulting scoring protocol is rubric-free: it uses overall scores without requesting criterion-level ratings. In the main Jev and Sol comparisons on SummEval summarization and HANNA story evaluation, PRISM and its learned-baseline variant significantly improve agreement with human rankings over uncalibrated scores while remaining competitive with rubric-based methods. A controlled SummEval comparison yields similar agreement for rubric-derived quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without reproducing rubric criteria. The learned coefficients reveal shared and opposing correction directions across judges.

documents.abstract: Abstract—The cross-organizational sharing of high-dimensional empirical datasets—such as electronic health records, financial credit transactions, and telecommunications telemetry—is fundamentally constrained by strict data governance legislation (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA). Heuristic sanitization methods (such as k-anonymity, l-diversity, and pseudo-anonymization) have repeatedly proven vulnerable to linkage and re-identification attacks. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)—encompassing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs)—offers the capability to synthesize structurally authentic surrogate populations. However, unconstrained generative models memorize sensitive training instances within their parameter weights, exposing downstream deployments to Membership Inference Attacks (MIA) and Attribute Disclosure Attacks. Differential Privacy (DP) provides the mathematical standard to guarantee bounded information leakage independent of adversarial prior knowledge. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Data Generation uniting Generative AI with Differential Privacy. We formalize the Renyi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting framework, model gradient perturbation dynamics under Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), and evaluate discrete marginal mechanisms (PrivBayes, PGM) alongside continuous generative models (DP-WGAN, DP-Diffusion). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise benchmarking testbed across three high-dimensional, sensitive datasets (MIMIC-III clinical records, German Credit, and Census PUMS). Our findings demonstrate that while unconstrained generative synthesis suffers a 74.2% membership inference vulnerability, DP-Diffusion governed by (epsilon = 1.0, delta = 10^-5) bounds attacker advantage to near-random guessing (51.8%) while preserving 91.4% downstream machine learning classification utility. Finally, we formulate open challenges in high-dimensional privacy budgeting, multi-modal alignment, and verified auditing frameworks. Index Terms—Differential Privacy (DP), Generative AI, Synthetic Data Generation, DP-SGD, Diffusion Models, Membership Inference Attacks (MIA), Renyi Differential Privacy, Data Governance.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

Abstract This article looks at the deregulation of US prison labor in the 1970s and 1980s, and the use of prison labor in information technology (IT) and digital electronics supply chains. The article, on one hand, locates the effort to deregulate prison labor in US electronics firms’ search for cheap labor enclaves and the uneven development of the postwar United States. At the same time, the article situiates this deregulatory turn in the progressive reforms of the 1970s. These reforms, which occurred first at the state and local levels, sought to promote prisoner welfare, provide opportunities for “self-help,” and rationalize the allocation of state and local resources in light of rising inflation. As such, the article complicates narratives of the rise of neoliberalism, which center issues like “lost confidence” in the efficacy of federal social welfare programs, breaches in public trust following Watergate, the 1973 oil shock, knock-on effects of New Deal and Great Society programs, or emerging “family values” and racist dog-whistle politics. It also frames the labor history of digital electronics in a way that supports an analysis of the relationship between capitalist development and US federalism aongside the particularities of firm-level motivation, insitutional inertia, and prevailing political ideology. Current discussions of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and corrections largely focus on the use of incarcerated persons to train AI algorithms or the use of AI systems to surveil prisoners. However, this article centers the growth of tech supply chains in the 1970s and 1980s as an important precursor to the development of contemporary AI technology and firms.

Choosing the right physician is a key challenge for patients seeking medical care. Physician recommendation systems identify relevant doctors, but patients still find it difficult to compare their profiles to make a decision. We formulate slate presentation optimization: given a patient's medical case and a fixed, ranked list of physicians, we generate short, case-specific summaries that make doctors easier to compare, while remaining grounded in the information in their profiles. To optimize physician presentations without relying on real patient interactions, we develop an offline framework that uses persona-conditioned LLMs to simulate patient choices. We generate patient personas from attributes extracted from each medical case and evaluate presentations for factual accuracy, relevance, naturalness and simulated patient choice. We also use a second LLM judge, unseen during optimization, to assess simulator-specific overfitting. We compare automatic prompt-level optimization with GEPA, parameter-level optimization with GRPO, and their combination across two model sizes. GRPO substantially outperforms GEPA in satisfying the full set of constraints, and its gains in simulated conversion persist under the unseen judge. GEPA alone brings smaller improvements, but using its optimized prompt to initialize GRPO speeds up training and achieves the highest simulated conversion. These results show that prompt-level and parameter-level optimization play complementary roles in improving how physician recommendations are presented.

documents.abstract: Abstract LLM agents increasingly call tools and take irreversible actions, yet the reasoning that licenses an action is rarely checked before execution. We present Proof-Carrying Agent Actions (PCAA) : each governed action carries a typed Action Certificate that a planner-independent checker must accept before execution. A trusted execution shim derives the obligation set and the irreversibility classification from an authoritative tool contract and binds the certificate to the exact invocation with a canonical SHA-256 commitment. The checker compares that context with the certificate, re-derives typed support (proof, belief, hypothesis, contingency, conflict, or no-progress), and validates formula-level inference rules. Irreversible actions require Proof for every declared licensing obligation. The checker accepts the two valid certificates and rejects all fifteen unsafe certificates in a semantic battery; four additional structural cases confirm rejection of argument substitution, precondition omission, and risk-flag downgrade. A microbenchmark of a three-obligation payment certificate measures 53.7 μs median and 65.7 μs p95 for construction, checking, serialization, and buffered local persistence. A stateful guardrail with the same certified-state predicate matches PCAA on safety; PCAA’s distinct contribution is a typed, replayable decision artifact. Guarantees are relative to trusted tool contracts: PCAA checks their use, not their real-world semantic correctness.

Generative AI has achieved remarkable success in de novo protein design, yet protein engineering typically begins with existing, characterized proteins. The primary demand is targeted local editing, e.g., engineering a specific region to optimize affinity, alter immunogenicity, or improve stability, while strictly preserving core catalytic motifs and overall scaffold integrity. However, no standardized framework currently exists for carrying out and evaluating such edits. In current generative-design workflows, researchers often need to manually specify complex low-level parameters and rely on repetitive, trial-and-error sampling and evaluation across generative backends to search for viable conformations. While large language models (LLMs) offer an intuitive interface to express these goals using natural language, prevailing structure-generation models cannot directly interpret high-level human instructions. To bridge this gap, we introduce PROTEAN, a standardized benchmark for text-guided protein structural editing. PROTEAN comprises 380 sub-tasks spanning six intervention families and evaluates a two-stage pipeline in which an LLM translates natural-language goals into backend-specific geometric constraints and a generative model remodels the protein backbone. A two-tier evaluation separates geometric compliance, including target attainment and off-target scope fidelity, from biophysical realizability assessed by inverse folding and refolding consistency. Across five frontier LLMs paired with three backends, strict end-to-end biophysical success starts at just 7.0%. Ablation studies show that LLM constraint compilation is already highly accurate, whereas the main bottlenecks are backend-specific scope leakage and refolding failure. PROTEAN provides an open testbed for developing autonomous, multi-backend macromolecular design agents.

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for vulnerability analysis, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of exploitation that depends on interactions among network protocol components. Such vulnerabilities arise from inconsistencies in message interpretation, timing, state, or trust assumptions across participants. We introduce ProtoArena, a black-box, multi-component, dynamic benchmark with 80 cross-component vulnerability-exploitation environments spanning 11 protocol and application domains and 7 attack categories. Tasks are primarily informed by published protocol-attack mechanisms. Agents interact with running systems through scoped interfaces to achieve security-effect objectives without target source code. Three information levels assess guided reproduction, exploitation with mechanism and topology context, and effect-directed black-box exploration. A hybrid verifier combines rule-based checks with LLM review of independently collected traffic and logs. We evaluate five LLMs. Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest observed success rates: 48.8% under L1 guidance and 12.5% under effect-directed black-box L3. In a separate DNSBomb optimization experiment, it achieves a peak downstream-response to average query-input byte-rate ratio exceeding 171,000 times. The results show that agents can achieve verifiable exploitation effects in some cross-component environments, but success with limited black-box information remains low and varies across domains and attack categories. All experiments use controlled, explicitly authorized targets; they do not test production systems or disclose previously unknown vulnerabilities.

This study examined public affairs communication in the era of climate change and artificial intelligence: strategies for policy and advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The technological determinism theory was anchored in this study. This study adopted a qualitative research method, utilising in-depth interviews to explore the role of artificial intelligence in public affairs communication for climate policy advocacy and governance in Nigeria. The population of the study consisted of 120 key stakeholders involved in climate policy advocacy and governance, including government officials, policymakers, environmental NGOs, media professionals and AI experts. The sample size comprised 20 purposively selected respondents with expertise in climate policy, artificial intelligence applications in governance and public affairs communication. The sampling technique used was purposive sampling, allowing the selection of individuals who possess specialized knowledge and experience relevant to the study. The method of data collection involves semi-structured, in-depth interviews and method of data analysis followed thematic analysis, where transcribed interview data were systematically coded to identify emerging patterns, themes and relationships. The findings revealed that, AI-driven tools significantly enhance public affairs communication by improving message dissemination, audience targeting and engagement strategies in climate advocacy. AI-powered chatbots, predictive analytics and automated content generation have been instrumental in personalizing climate messages and countering misinformation. The study concluded that AI has emerged as a transformative tool in public affairs communication, enabling more effective climate advocacy through targeted messaging, audience engagement and misinformation management. However, its full potential can only be realised if challenges such as algorithmic bias, inadequate digital infrastructure and the need for human-centred communication strategies are addressed. The study recommended that Policymakers and communication professionals should invest in AIdriven tools while ensuring ethical guidelines and human-centred approaches to enhance climate advocacy in Nigeria

Abstract The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.

documents.abstract: Practical quantum programs interleave quantum and classical computation: classical data shape the quantum operations that are performed, and measurement outcomes shape the classical computation that follows. Formal verification of such programs in a proof assistant requires mechanizing a program logic that handles this interplay consistently at every level, from the mathematics of quantum mechanics, through program syntax and semantics, to specifications and proof rules. Such mechanizations, along with the program proofs built on them, typically require substantial manual effort. We present QEDIA, a framework for verifying quantum programs with classical variables in Lean 4. At its foundation is an open library that formalizes the quantum Hoare logic QHL+ across all these levels and proves the logic sound for both partial and total correctness. We construct the library and the program proofs, under human supervision, using an LLM-based prover agent, whose general-purpose core we extend for quantum program verification. We illustrate QEDIA with verified programs including the quantum Fourier transform, phase estimation, repeat-until-success circuits, and Hamiltonian simulation.

Quantum Sociodynamics (QSD) is introduced as a computational method for modelling symbolic influence and trust in artificial-intelligence-supported sustainable city transitions. Its central object, the Symbolic Mediation Field, represents how actor orientations, source–audience relations and communication histories shape signal effects. Actor states are encoded by complex variables ψi, symbolic transport by U(1) link variables Uij, signed coupling by qi and external interventions by Ji. Gauge-invariant measures capture local alignment, path transport and loop holonomy. Formal analysis establishes invariance under local re-description, path independence under zero holonomy and a classical DeGroot–Friedkin–Johnsen limit. Deterministic simulations demonstrate response reversal, order effects and persistent relational change after institutional shocks. A 27-record heat-pump corpus illustrates application to AI-assisted urban decarbonisation governance and identifies validation requirements.

The post-pandemic labor landscape has witnessed the rise of "quiet quitting"—a behavioral phenomenon where employees strictly adhere to their contractual job descriptions while withholding discretionary extra-role behaviors, discretionary effort, and voluntary over-time involvement. While often framed by mainstream media as an expression of worker apathy, this study conceptualizes quiet quitting as a structural symptom of workplace burnout, organizational injustice, and systemic psychological contract breach. Through a comprehensive evaluation using Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, Social Exchange Theory (SET), and the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, this paper examines the cascading operational, psychological, and financial impacts of quiet quitting on long-term organizational sustainability. I argue that relying on short-term extra-role extraction undermines triple-bottom-line organizational health. Ultimately, quiet quitting is not an expression of employee indolence, but a strategic self-preservation mechanism in response to prolonged work stress, unmet organizational expectations, and systemic burnout. Finally, an evidence-based strategic framework is offered to realign managerial practices, work-design architectures, and performance metrics to foster sustainable workforce resilience as well as recommendations are posited.

Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.

Modern conversational information access systems continuously extract user information from conversations to build user profiles for personalized retrieval. As user profiles accumulate over time, they inevitably become noisy, making effective user profile denoising a fundamental challenge. Existing personalized conversational query reformulation methods rely on the black-box reasoning capability of LLMs to expand the original query with relevant user profile phrases, producing a verbose query for retrieval. Such rewrite-then-retrieve pipelines reduce user profile denoising to the explicit selection of profile phrases in the sparse token space, separating personalization from downstream relevance modeling. Consequently, they often fail to identify user information that is truly beneficial for retrieval. To enable retrieval-aware user profile denoising, we propose Personalized Conversational Dense Retrieval (PCDR), which learns to jointly project the conversation history and user profile into a latent embedding space dedicated to retrieval. By inheriting the context denoising capability from conversational dense retrievers, PCDR requires only a handful of personalized relevance annotations for training. We evaluate PCDR on the iKAT 2026 tasks, where it serves as the core retrieval component of a conversational AI agent assisting users with complex information needs.

This study proposes an uncertainty-aware collision-risk evaluation framework for the safe navigation of autonomous ships. Target-ship information obtained from the Automatic Identification System (AIS) and radar is characterized by discrete update intervals and measurement uncertainty, which can degrade situational awareness and collision-avoidance decision-making. To address this problem, an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) was used to fuse AIS and radar data and estimate target-ship states and associated uncertainties in real time. The resulting state-estimation covariance was incorporated into the Quaternion Ship Domain (QSD) to construct a probabilistic ship domain that reflects target-position uncertainty. Based on this domain, Probabilistic Collision Exposure (PCE) was defined as a velocity-space collision-exposure metric representing the proportion of collision-causing velocity vectors within the own ship's reachable velocity set, while Expected Collision Energy (ECE) was formulated to incorporate the potential collision consequence. The framework was evaluated through MMG-based simulations involving head-on, starboard crossing, nonlinear maneuvering, and three-target multiple-encounter scenarios under delayed and noisy sensing conditions. In the nonlinear maneuvering scenario, the target-position error remained within approximately 5 m, with an average error of approximately 3 m. Compared with the conventional Collision Risk Index (CRI), PCE showed substantially lower residual risk after the closest point of approach (CPA) in the representative head-on and starboard crossing scenarios. The post-CPA residual area-under-the-curve (AUC) ratios were 2.21% and 0.59% for PCE in the head-on and starboard crossing scenarios, respectively, compared with 32.80% and 40.48% for CRI. The three-target scenario further demonstrated target-specific collision-exposure evaluation and simultaneous multi-target avoidance, while the implemented framework maintained its nominal 10-Hz system update cycle across the evaluated single-target and multi-target simulations.

When a clinical AI system’s output differs from a human clinician’s judgment, what follows is consequential and underspecified. Current AI interfaces offer only a narrow lane for what happens next: they present the AI output (and its associated potential divergence) as an adjudicative choice for a human to accept, override, or modify. In practice, collapsing this human-AI interaction into a single output inadvertently obscures what happens in a potential divergence event (Fig. 1 ) which can be characterized along three axes: What the workflow and interface allow the clinician to see and do ( structural axis), what information each side brought to the interaction ( informational axis), and how the clinician engaged with the AI’s reasoning rather than only its output ( behavioral axis). When clinical judgment and AI output diverge, clinicians must ultimately decide what to recommend and how to explain their recommendation to the patient, consider their autonomy, accountability, and liability, and bear moral responsibility 1 . A recent systematic review of AI ethics in nursing and midwifery found that AI challenges the role of health professionals not through replacement, but through subtle reconfiguration of the activities that count as care and that emphasis on AI efficiency may risk certain relational aspects of care less visible and valued 2 . Because clinicians often cannot see how an AI system reached its output, they are left to choose between that AI output and their own judgment. Clinicians are told to be the “human in the loop” but are typically given no method for doing so beyond “exercising their judgment” 3 . Efforts to make AI output both more technically explainable and human interpretable - have not directly correlated with improved clinical decisions and have sometimes created false confidence in incorrect AI output 4 .

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models (LLMs) are transforming clinical decision support systems (CDSS) from traditional discrete predictions into fluent, context-aware clinical narrative generation. Although these capabilities substantially improve the efficiency of clinical workflows, they also introduce distinctive cognitive challenges: highly fluent and seemingly plausible medical narratives may reshape the way physicians construct clinical meaning and make analytic judgments. This perspective paper introduces the concept of Narrative Cognitive Substitution (NCS), proposed as a testable mid-level theoretical construct, which describes the hypothesized shift in human cognition from active hypothesis generation to passive retrospective validation when GenAI outputs pre-organize diagnostic reasoning and therapeutic pathways. We further propose a Skill Evolution Framework that characterizes the potential effects of GenAI on physician competence across five trajectories: Augmentation, Restructuring, Deskilling, Never-skilling, and Mis-skilling. In addition, we analyze the resulting Accountability Gap: although algorithmic outputs are increasingly embedded in clinical decision-making, decision influence is distributed across clinicians, institutions, developers, and deployers, yet professional accountability and final decision authority remain formally concentrated on the individual physician. To address these systemic challenges, we propose a human-centered governance framework —presented as design hypotheses requiring prospective evaluation— encompassing user interface design (embedding risk-adaptive cognitive friction), medical education (establishing targeted, protected AI-free reasoning exercises (“Reasoning Cleanrooms”)), and institutional policies (implementing substantive human oversight and algorithmovigilance). We argue that the goal of digital health governance should not be to maximize automation, but rather to safeguard human cognitive agency, diagnostic vigilance, and layered, distributed accountability within AI-enabled healthcare systems.
