documents.abstract: To distinguish between “text improvement” and “cognitive gain” in generative-AI-assisted second language learning, this study proposes a Multimodal Intervention-Aware Temporal Graph Network (MITG-Net). The method integrates human-AI dialogue, revision trajectories, behavioral logs, and learner attributes. Through intervention-conditioned dynamic weighting and heterogeneous temporal graph modeling, it captures the relationships among prompts, feedback, revisions, and transfer, and jointly performs intervention-effect recognition and learning-behavior-pattern discovery. Experiments were conducted on 744 learning sessions collected from 186 undergraduates at three universities. MITG-Net achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.816 and a weighted Kappa of 0.854, outperforming the strongest baseline, HGT, by 3.4 percentage points in Macro-F1. Removing behavioral logs and revision trajectories reduced Macro-F1 by 0.054 and 0.045, respectively. The model identified five behavior patterns. Among them, the strategy-transfer application pattern achieved an average effect level of 2.78 and a transfer score of 0.82, substantially higher than the 1.36 and 0.31 obtained by the AI-dominated direct-adoption pattern. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively recognize cognitive intervention effects and provide interpretable evidence for personalized support in second language learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the learning ecology by positioning AI as a cognitive partner that supports personalisation, feedback, problem-solving, and creativity. This transformation necessitates a reconstruction of the concept of self-actualisation, as some human cognitive activities can be delegated to AI. This study aims to analyse the transformation of self actualisation, identify the conditions that strengthen or hinder it, and formulate a conceptual framework for self-actualisation in AI-based learning. This study employs a qualitative library research approach using an integrative literature review design. The findings indicate that GenAI is paradoxical in nature: it can serve as a cognitive scaffold that strengthens autonomy, competence, self-regulation, creativity, metacognition, and epistemic agency, while also potentially encouraging cognitive offloading, dependence, and the weakening of cognitive autonomy. This study proposes the Reflective-Relational Self Actualisation Framework in AI Learning Ecologies (RRSA-AILE), which encompasses autonomy, competence, relatedness, epistemic agency, metacognitive reflexivity, generative creativity, and ethical responsibility. Theoretically, RRSA-AILE integrates humanism, Self-Determination Theory, Self-Regulated Learning, and learner agency. Practically, the framework provides a foundation for AI-enhanced learning that is augmentative, reflective, and centred on human agency.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown strong potential for remote sensing understanding, yet reliable reasoning remains challenging when tasks require fine-grained visual grounding and multi-step inference. Existing approaches typically rely on either costly pre-constructed reasoning trajectories or self-generated signals such as response consistency, which can reinforce shared errors and provide unreliable supervision. We introduce \textbf{Reasoning--Diagnosis Self-Evolution (ReDiS)}, a framework that separates reasoning exploration from candidate evaluation while allowing the two processes to evolve jointly. ReDiS instantiates two role-specific experts from a shared multimodal backbone: a \textbf{Reasoner} that explores diverse visual evidence--answer candidates and a \textbf{Diagnoser} that jointly evaluates the complete candidate set and provides credibility-aware feedback. As the Reasoner evolves, it exposes new candidate distributions and failure modes; the Diagnoser adapts to these changes and, in turn, reshapes the learning signal for subsequent exploration. To handle groups in which all sampled answers are incorrect and group-relative advantages vanish, we further introduce \textbf{Failure-Triggered Recovery (FTR)}, which provides minimal outcome-level correction without prescribing intermediate reasoning trajectories. Experiments on LHRS-Bench, MME-RS, and CHOICE show consistent improvements over Qwen3.5 backbones at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B scales. ReDiS improves category-averaged accuracy by 6.47 percentage points at 0.8B, while ReDiS-4B achieves the highest average performance among the compared remote sensing MLLMs.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has given rise to increasingly more realistic fake contents such as deepfake faces, hardly distinguishable from real faces. However, evidence has shown that social evaluations of real faces are also able to impact the detection of deepfake faces. The present study aimed at applying for the first time the valence-dominance model for face evaluation on deepfake faces. Moreover, the impact of its thirteen attributes on deepfake detection performances was investigated. Specifically, 311 participants categorised 120 faces (50% real, 50% deepfake created ad hoc by Diffusion Model technology) and rated faces in regards to one of the attributes. Principal Component Analysis was applied in order to validate the valence-dominance model on deepfake faces, and a Brunswikian lens model was applied to understand how each attribute contributes to a face being judged as deepfake. Results replicated the valence-dominance model on real faces as well as on faces categorized by participants as deepfake, but not on actual deepfake faces. Finally, the indirect effects of the Brunswikian model revealed caringness and intelligence to impair detection of deepfake stimuli, whilst weirdness was revealed to be a positive indirect predictor, being positively associated with higher detection accuracy of deepfake faces. Our results shed, for the first time, light into the differential cognitive processing of deepfake faces and their social evaluation whilst also providing novel insight into underlying mechanisms associated with deepfake detection. Interdisciplinary implications regarding the theoretical and applied contribution are discussed.

ABSTRACT Chronic sleep debt impairs cognitive processes, stress regulation, and immune homeostasis, while sustained cognitive engagement induces mental fatigue. However, it remains unclear how chronically insufficient sleep in real-life conditions accelerates the onset of mental fatigue during prolonged cognitive activity—and whether daytime napping can buffer these effects. This study investigated the combined effects of chronic sleep debt and extended cognitive engagement on cognitive fatigue and salivary neuro-immune and neurotrophic markers in an ecologically valid context. Compared with controls, participants with chronic sleep debt showed pronounced declines in Psychomotor Vigilance Task performance (reaction time and number of lapses) across both time-on-task and time-on-week and showed higher commission rates in the executive Go-NoGo task. These morning impairments were partially attenuated in the participants who practiced afternoon chronic naps, and the reduction in lapses was correlated with nap frequency. Biologically, chronic sleep debt was associated with a blunted morning cortisol response, an increase in IL-1β and IL-6, and a reduction in BDNF levels, but not observed in either the Control or Sleep-Debt + Nap groups. In the Sleep-Debt group, IL-1β levels were positively correlated with sustained attention deficits. Chronic sleep debt increased attentional fatigability without exacerbating executive decline, an effect that may be driven by neuro-inflammatory processes and effectively alleviated by regular daytime napping. Importantly, these findings indicate that chronic afternoon napping may confer protective and long-lasting restorative benefits observable in morning assessments, reflecting effects that persist over a 24-hour period.

Artificial intelligence is transforming the knowledge structure of medicine and reshaping how physicians are trained across undergraduate medical education, residency, and continuing professional development. As predictive algorithms increasingly perform pattern recognition tasks once central to clinical expertise, the definition of “core medical knowledge” is shifting toward data literacy, probabilistic reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and ethical oversight of intelligent systems. This chapter examines how AI-assisted and AI-integrated learning environments are altering the roles of memorization, diagnostic reasoning, and clinical decision making, while creating new expectations for physicians as interpreters of algorithmic outputs rather than sole generators of diagnostic insight. It explores emerging educational models incorporating simulation, adaptive tutoring systems, multimodal decision support tools, and lifelong learning infrastructures embedded within digital health systems. Ultimately, reimagining medical education requires balancing technological capability with human judgment so that clinicians remain central to safe, equitable, and patient-centered care in an increasingly automated healthcare environment.

documents.abstract: Operational reporting for high-performance computing (HPC) facilities requires combining information from monitoring services, schedulers, incident and maintenance records, storage measurements, periodic reports, and operator investigations. Producing a reliable report requires more than retrieving relevant records: the evidence must refer to the correct system, metric definition, time period, and source of authority. We present REPORT-OPS, a hybrid reporting agent in which an LLM interprets requests, plans evidence collection, evaluates possible explanations, and drafts reports, while author-seeded operational policies and automated checks determine whether the available evidence supports the requested conclusion. Depending on the evidence state, the system answers the request, reports a qualified conclusion, or withholds an unsupported claim. During offline refinement, an LLM critic proposes bounded policy changes that a human approves or rejects without editing; accepted candidates are promoted only after automated target, held-out, and regression testing. We evaluate REPORT-OPS on 68 sanitized reporting queries constructed from 50 base scenarios in a frozen HPC operational corpus, using three agent models and two LLM judges. REPORT-OPS achieves 68.63% Pass@80, compared with 7.02% for the strongest retrieval baseline. Evidence gating increases claim-support precision from 40.58% to 90.06%. On the 13-query explanatory subset, explanation accuracy reaches 55.54%. Across five rounds of human-supervised refinement, localized policy updates correct 91.17% of targeted failures and improve performance on related held-out cases by 9.33 percentage points, with no observed regression breaks under release gating. These results demonstrate improved evidence-grounded reporting and within-environment policy reuse; they do not establish unrestricted causal discovery or cross-facility generalization.

Abstract Objective To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. Design Systematic review and meta-research analysis. Data sources Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. Eligibility criteria Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. Main outcome measures Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis—LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. Results The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations. Trial reports were predominantly small sample, single site randomised studies published between 2024 and 2025, spanning diverse clinical specialties and primarily targeting patient facing education and management recommendations. Mean reporting completeness was modest across eligible trial reports (TRIPOD-LLM 40%, CONSORT 2025 44%, CONSORT-AI 59%, CHART 52%), trial protocols (SPIRIT 2025 51%, SPIRIT-AI 57%), and trial registrations (WHO Trial Registration Dataset 61%). Clinical trial reports of LLM interventions prioritise narrative framing and commentary over the methodological detail needed for replication, risk-of-bias assessment, and governance of model performance over time. Critical methodological elements for reproducibility, including data and intervention provenance, input preprocessing, model versioning and access modality, inference parameters, output postprocessing, as well as protocol, data, and code access, were inconsistently reported. Harms planning, monitoring, and reporting were often incompletely reported, limiting the critical appraisal of the safety of LLM interventions in healthcare. Conclusion Clinical trials of LLM interventions show modest adherence to established reporting guidelines, with persistent underreporting of LLM specific methodological details, reproducibility artefacts (protocols, data, code), and harms reporting required to support reproducibility and confident appraisal of safety risks before their clinical translation.

documents.abstract: This article reconstructs a history of language, reason, and practical activity from Augustine through Kant, Hegel, Marx, the European linguistic turn, and analytic philosophy in order to formulate the concept of reproductive iden tity. Reproductive identity is not sameness, a fixed inner essence, or the final conceptual possession of the world. It is the historically open, materially conditioned work through which embodied individuals and communities sustain, repair, and develop the relations that enable their continuation. Augustine’s psychological trinity supplies an early grammar of memory, understanding, and will or love; Kant clarifies the conditions of judgment and practical reason; Hegel understands concept and reality as mutually realised in activity; and Marx translates this movement into the communal metabolism through which human beings reproduce life in and through nature. The linguistic turn and an alytic philosophy provide indispensable accounts of disclosure, difference, reference, truth, use, and normativity. The section on analytic philosophy distinguishes formal validity from situated inquiry and reconstructs practical reason as both normatively articulated and causally efficacious. Neither tradition, however, can settle the material and in stitutional conditions of the forms of life in which language works. The final sections develop ecological democracy and politically subordinate artificial intelligence as institutional consequences of the argument. Artificial intelligence is treated not as a sovereign subject but as a reversible public infrastructure whose legitimacy depends on ecological admissibility, traceability, contestability, repair, and the common reproduction of internal and external nature.

Abstract Despite growing clinical adoption of artificial intelligence in radiology, fewer than one in five commercially available models are cleared for paediatric use. Existing systems are trained predominantly on adult data and generalize poorly to neonates, yet efficient strategies for repurposing them without data sharing or large-scale local data curation are lacking. Here we present an international retrospective study of neonatal chest radiographs from 30 neonatal intensive care units across 20 countries and territories, evaluating continual learning as a privacy-preserving approach to adapt a deep learning model for adult endotracheal tube assessment to neonatal care. Each hospital contributed 50 radiographs for sequential model retraining without centralized data pooling. Continual learning achieved lower anatomical landmark localization error (0.67 cm versus 1.29 cm for hospital-specific fine-tuning and 4.30 cm for adult-only models) at 29 of 30 sites, with improved detection of deep intubations at 27 of 30 sites. These findings demonstrate that privacy-preserving collaborative learning can address critical gaps in paediatric AI deployment.

documents.abstract: Rapid situational awareness is a cornerstone of effective civil protection and disaster response, demanding highly resilient localization and decision-support capabilities under challenging environmental conditions. This paper presents RESCUE-AR (Responsive Sensor-Fusion for Civil-Protection and Disaster Response Using Mobile Augmented Reality), a conceptual and methodological framework for mobile Augmented Reality (AR) systems designed to support emergency operations through heterogeneous and adaptive sensor fusion. This work formalizes the mathematical and algorithmic architecture of the RESCUE-AR framework, establishing an adaptive multi-sensor measurement fusion strategy, integrating Visual SLAM, IMU, depth sensing, and GNSS data to enhance robustness in environments affected by occlusion, signal degradation, and dynamic change. The framework is grounded in a systematic literature review that identifies the limitations of single-sensor and fixed-weight fusion approaches in disaster scenarios and motivates the adoption of adaptive fusion strategies. Validation is conducted through a structured user-centered evaluation, employing standardized questionnaires to assess usability, cognitive workload, perceived accuracy, trust, and operational suitability for first responders. The results indicate strong perceived utility, reduced cognitive load, and high confidence in AR-assisted decision-making, supporting the potential of adaptive sensor-fusion-based mobile AR as a viable and scalable decision-support tool for civil protection and disaster response.

Background/Objectives: This study utilizes machine learning (ML) models integrated with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to perform a retrospective analysis of factors associated with tuberculosis (TB) treatment duration and outcomes. Methods: Two datasets comprising completed TB patient records from a Malaysian hospital were analyzed. Significant features were identified using Pearson correlation for treatment duration and the Boruta algorithm for treatment outcome. Support Vector Regressor (SVR) was used to evaluate treatment duration, while Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost were evaluated for treatment outcome classification. SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) was integrated to enhance model interpretability. Results: On the primary dataset (Dataset A), SVRPearson demonstrated the best performance for treatment duration (MAE = 44.18 days, R2 = 0.54), although performance decreased on the external dataset (Dataset B: MAE = 71.33 days, R2 = 0.11), partly due to missing feature imputations. For treatment outcome classification, XGBoostBoruta achieved an accuracy of 99.20% on Dataset A and 97.34% on Dataset B. SHAP feature attribution indicated that treatment outcome was the primary contributor to treatment duration, whereas treatment status and treatment duration were the dominant features contributing to the treatment outcome model. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the value of explainable machine learning for characterizing factors associated with TB treatment duration and outcomes in completed treatment episodes and supporting retrospective clinical audit and post hoc case interpretation.

The global prevalence of chronic diseases is becoming increasingly severe, and traditional care models are confronted with multiple challenges, including uneven distribution of medical resources, insufficient continuity of care, and inadequate patient self-management capacity. The rapid iteration of digital technologies and the catalyst of the COVID-19 pandemic have driven chronic disease care into a new phase of digital transformation. Based on relevant studies published from 2021 to 2026, this paper structures its analysis around a core logical framework: evidence-based evidence, care models, population adaptability and practical implementation. It systematically reviews the core technical systems and innovative characteristics of care models in digital chronic disease care, deeply analyzes the adaptive differences across diverse populations and disease types, and conducts critical reflections from the perspectives of evidence quality, health equity, clinical applicability, and homogeneity in intervention design. Finally, it puts forward future development directions centered on precision, localization, equity, and integration. The study reveals that digital chronic disease care has formed four core technological systems in application: intelligent sensing, digital behavioral intervention, immersive technology, and artificial intelligence (AI) and big data. Care models demonstrate innovative trends of nurse leadership, multi-dimensional collaboration, and caregiver empowerment. Nevertheless, prominent issues persist, such as insufficient high-quality evidence, a striking digital divide, difficulties in clinical integration, and a lack of personalized design. In the future, deep integration of technological innovation with clinical demands, enhanced targeted interventions for vulnerable populations, implementation of localized long-term studies, and improvement of policy and ethical guarantee systems are required. These efforts will promote the shift of digital chronic disease care from technology-driven to evidence-driven and demand-driven models, ultimately improving the overall efficiency of chronic disease management and health equity.

Generative retrieval (GR) has emerged as a strong candidate generator for sequential recommendation as language models and semantic-item identifiers have improved. However, GR is not a uniformly stronger replacement of dense retrieval (DR) in online retail candidate generation. We examine their differences on two Amazon Toys datasets under different metrics. GR leads on best relevant item value among users both methods cover, while DR leads on exact-target recall and relevant value across the ranked list. With deep analysis, we find that popularity contributes the most to GR's measured value lead. Adding the same static item value to DR in one reranking step reverses this lead and keeps recall above GR. Finally, on an industrial-scale internal e-commerce dataset with LLM-judged relevance, we show that a 14B SID-LLM still underperforms a $47\times$ smaller dense encoder.

A fundamental limitation of current predictive maintenance is the inability to transform prognostic uncertainty into actionable decisions, which often leads to either wasteful early interventions or catastrophic failures in aero-engines. To address this, we propose the Risk-Aware Predictive Maintenance (RAPM) framework consisting of four integrated components: a probabilistic stacked sparse autoencoder that extracts degradation features while providing distributional remaining useful life (RUL) predictions; a Monte Carlo Dropout module with Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) that summarizes lower-tail predictive risk and produces a conservative RUL estimate for decision making; a locally deployed large language model (Qwen2.5-3B) that abstracts numerical uncertainty into discrete semantic risk levels, enabling interpretable reward shaping; and a Proximal Policy Optimization agent trained with curriculum learning to handle long-horizon sparse-reward maintenance optimization. On the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 benchmark, RAPM achieves a 96.0% optimal stopping rate with no late interventions or failure events compared with 90.2% for the strongest independent maintenance baseline. Under controlled substitution with LSTM-MCD, Transformer-MCD, CNN-MCD, and Deep Ensemble prognostic backbones, the same CVaR-LLM-PPO decision architecture maintains optimal stopping rates of 92.4–95.2% with no late interventions or failure events. Within the matched Rule-PPO ablation, CVaR increases the mean optimal stopping rate from 92.0% to 95.0% under unperturbed conditions, which is a gain of 3.0 percentage points. Under Gaussian sensor noise (σ=0.05), the gain reaches 9.0 percentage points, from 73.0% to 82.0%. These results demonstrate that the decision benefit of RAPM extends across independently trained prognostic models.

Prompting is a widely used method for adapting general-purpose LLMs to domain-specific tasks. Effective prompts can be tedious to create manually, so prompt writing is increasingly handed to LLMs, with recent work training LLMs to write prompts for other models. These techniques either write prompts without observing how the task model behaves, blind to the failure modes the prompt should address, or must run alongside the task LLM at inference time, adding overhead to every query. Neither reflects how prompt engineering is often practiced. To close this gap, we introduce Reinforcement Learned Prompt Engineering (RLPE), which trains a model to analyze traces of a separate task model and write a prompt targeting the failures it observes. RLPE rewards the trained model strictly on prompt performance, so it learns the prompting strategies that improve the task model. The prompt is generated once and reused across the task, so inference does not require the trained model. Since RLPE needs only query access to the model it prompts, it is also compatible with closed-source models. We apply RLPE to Enigmata, BIG-Bench Extra Hard, and PlanBench. We train a 9B-parameter model that writes better prompts than state-of-the-art frontier models (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-opus-5) and prompt optimizers (GEPA and TextGrad) on 2/3 benchmarks. Although the model is never explicitly trained to iterate on prompts, this capability emerges at a level that matches or beats frontier models. The learned prompting capability also generalizes, with the trained model improving task models 6x larger than the one it trained with, including ones from entirely different model families, and matching claude-opus-5 on a fourth benchmark held out from training.

This dataset (roboboss_shared_data.csv) contains survey responses examining professionals' attitudes toward knowledge work, algorithmic management (ALMA), artificial intelligence, and leadership. The data is structured in a long format to facilitate repeated-measures analysis of hypothetical management scenarios. In these scenarios, respondents evaluated different management styles (positive, neutral, negative) executed by either human or machine (AI) managers. The dataset includes demographic information, organizational context, multi-item sum scores for psychological and workplace constructs, and scenario-based evaluations recorded on a 5-point Likert scale. Variable names and most categorical labels are in English, while specific Likert-scale response options retain their original Finnish phrasing. More details of the data table can be found in roboboss_shared_data_description.md. Codes used in computing statistical results can be found at folder statistical_analyses for stages 1-3. Final statistical results can be found at subfolder statistical_analyses/model_fits

documents.abstract: Abstract - The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and biotechnology is revolutionizing scientific research, healthcare, and industrial applications. This paper examines how AI techniques, like computer vision, machine learning, deep learning, and NLP, are revolutionizing important biotechnology fields like drug discovery, genomics, personalized medicine, agricultural innovation, and industrial bioprocessing. AI enables faster data analysis, accurate prediction of biological behaviors, and automation of complex tasks, significantly accelerating the pace of innovation. We also discuss commonly used AI tools in biotechnology and highlight the growth of AI-driven biotech startups. The incorporation of AI presents a number of obstacles despite its transformative potential, such as the requirement for transparent algorithms, ethical issues, and data privacy concerns. The goal of the article is to provide a thorough review of the state of affairs, recent developments, and potential future progress in the nexus of biotechnology and artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: Egocentric multimodal assistants see through the user's eyes and guide what the user does next, so their outputs directly shape physical actions, including those that affect bystanders. Yet existing safety evaluations do not distinguish whom a response would harm, and score only whether a model refuses. Pooling all harms into one refusal rate hides two failures: a model may protect one target but not another, and it may refuse without understanding the risk, or understand it and comply anyway. We present STOU, a benchmark of 2,902 egocentric video-audio and video-text queries whose potential harm targets the user (Self), co-present individuals (The Others), or society at large (Others). Our evaluation decouples safety understanding from refusal behavior: beyond refusal, we score whether the model recognizes the user's intent, the presence and target of harm, and its downstream consequences. Across 10 open and closed source omnimodal and multimodal LLMs, we find that refusal varies systematically with the harm target, and that models often recognize a harm yet still assist with it. These results show that refusal rates alone cannot certify an assistant as safe, and that safety alignment must account for who would be harmed. Project page: https://onedayoneyeah.github.io/safety-for-whom

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in clinical decision making, raising complex questions about safety, accountability, and regulatory oversight when algorithmic recommendations contribute to harm. Unlike traditional medical devices, many AI systems evolve over time, operate across institutional boundaries, and depend on dynamic datasets, making responsibility for errors distributed among clinicians, developers, and healthcare organizations. This chapter examines emerging regulatory frameworks governing clinical AI, including validation standards, post-market surveillance requirements, and lifecycle oversight approaches developed by agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and international regulators. It also explores how clinicians can evaluate predictive models before adoption by assessing transparency, calibration, fairness, and generalizability. Understanding shared accountability in AI-assisted care is essential to ensuring safe implementation without slowing innovation. Ultimately, effective governance will depend on collaboration among clinicians, engineers, institutions, and regulators to create trustworthy systems that improve outcomes while protecting patients.

documents.abstract: TypeSafe AI's Jev is a new kind of safety judge. It generates no text and no label: it answers questions the developer defines in advance and returns a probability for each answer. The vendor admits that adversarial input can change these answers but gives no numbers. In this paper, we present the first controlled adversarial evaluation of Jev. We build a test harness that sends every system the same payload under the same policy, and run it on four public-data tasks, from rule-based ones (input moderation, injection detection, routing) to a judgment-based one (phishing detection), with fifty attack variants from thirteen families. The targets are Jev, five GPT and GLM judges, and two local classifiers (Llama Guard 3, Prompt Guard 2). We find that Jev is the most robust system on input moderation: eight forgeries of its structured input bypass none of its decisions, and a sentence asking only why someone might make a harmful request bypasses 9% of its blocks, against 56% for GPT-6 Astra. On phishing detection. However, the same forgeries bypass 19-29% of the emails it flags, and even without attack Jev detects only 62% of phishing emails, against 77-81% for the GLM judges. Jev is also the fastest judge, but it flags the most benign requests (27%). The local classifiers fail differently: a training-example statement makes Llama Guard 3 miss 62% of the phishing it had flagged. These results suggest that Jev resists attacks on tasks with a clear rule to check but is more exposed on tasks that call for an overall judgment.

This research paper investigates the severe educational resource scarcity in Balochistan, and its impact on student learning outcomes and career Preparation. Regardless of growing youth populations, public and private educational institutions in the region face widespread systemic challenges. Based on survey data his study shows how local education falls short in basic school facilities, modern technology subjects, practical career training, global exam access, college degree tracks, and extracurricular activities. Specifically, over 69% of local students rely on government schools plagued by broken facilities, missing basic utilities, and unmonitored teacher absenteeism. Furthermore, institutions suffer from a complete absence of modern fields like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Robotics, poor quality in practical computer-based training, extreme financial barriers in advanced schooling (A-Levels), a total lack of international test centers (SAT/TOEFL), and a major shortage of sports, public speaking, and student development programs. The paper also highlights severe gender disparities caused by unsafe transport options and domestic burdens. To bridge the gap between classroom instruction and modern market requirements, this study proposes key policy recommendations, including targeted infrastructure investment, institutional accountability, curriculum modernization, fully equipped science and computer laboratories, structured career counseling, extracurricular programs (sports and Model United Nations), and safe, dedicated transportation for female students.

Scientific reasoning moves beyond natural language. The search for a discovery runs across sequences, structures, fields, omics, images and measurements, while language models reason mainly in text. This Perspective sets out four proposals from the Scinetics team. First, we define science tokens: modality-appropriate units of scientific information, spanning native discrete symbols, typed values, continuous representations and learned, decodable codes. A shared interface for these representations would let one model read, write and reason across modalities, so that a chain of science tokens operates on scientifically meaningful states, not on descriptions of them. Second, we define Scientific Super Intelligence (SSI) as a joint crossover: one frozen model that outperforms vertical specialists, such as the AlphaFold series on protein structure prediction, on their own tasks, and outperforms general large language models of the same size on broad scientific reasoning. Capacity, published training precedents, data inventories and compute place the first test of that crossover at 100–300 billion parameters and 10–30 trillion training tokens. Third, we propose ScienceRSI (Science Recursive Self- Improvement) as the route to that window. Following the AI4AI pattern, each larger generation is trained on data that the smaller generation before it produced: the earlier model generates candidate reasoning, screens it and keeps what passes, and in science that screening can be done by a simulation, a database or an experiment. Training this way reduces the dependence on scarce human-written scientific reasoning data and shortens each iteration. Fourth, we propose science-token economics, which separates metered computation from the value of evidence-labelled, reusable scientific assets.

The complete screening record behind a structured narrative review of contextual determinants of health AI effectiveness, submitted to the Journal of Medical Systems in October 2026.The deposit contains every unique record retrieved by the review's search (n = 5,178) with its source database, external identifiers, embedding-similarity score, screening band, and the decision recorded at each of the three screening stages; the 192 records carried forward to author verification with all three stage decisions side by side; and the 47 records confirmed as meeting the eligibility criterion.It is published because the review's screening-priority ranking cannot be independently re-executed: the embedding model and the composition of the reference set were not recorded at the time. The similarity threshold (0.6522) and the resulting bands are reported, but the scores cannot be regenerated. Publishing the full record makes the consequences of that ranking auditable record by record even though the ranking itself is not reproducible.No abstract text from the retrieved records is included; abstracts are the copyright of their publishers. The files carry identifiers, bibliographic metadata, similarity scores and the authors' own decisions, which is sufficient to recompute every flow count reported in the manuscript.The review is not a systematic review. Its search was used to construct a transparent evidence pool for purposive theoretical sampling rather than to identify studies exhaustively, and the figure of 47 is a count within the author-verified pool, not a count of all eligible studies in the databases searched. The README documents the limitations of the record in full.

documents.abstract: The author presents newly derived differential constitutive relations (equations) of the second fractional order for complex, higher-level rheological models of fractional-type viscoelastic materials with piezoelectric properties. These newly derived differential equations are of the second fractional order and incorporate Caputo differential operators of the first and second fractional orders. The lecturer outlines an approximate analytical methodology for solving these second-fractional-order differential equations, employing the Laplace transform, expansion into power series with respect to the complex Laplace parameter, and the properties of the convolution of three functions. This methodology yields approximate analytical solutions for the mew derived second-fractional-order differential constitutive equations governing these complex, higher-level rheological materials. These approximate analytical solutions simultaneously serve as integral constitutive relations, establishing the link between normal stresses and axial strains in these complex, higher-level rheological models of fractional-type viscoelastic materials with piezoelectric properties. The theoretical analytical results obtained pertain to complex fractional-type material models, specifically the second-level complexity Letherish-Faraday model for a fractional-type viscoelastic material with piezoelectric properties; The Jeffreys-Faraday model represents a second-level complexity rheological model for a fractional-type viscoelastic material with piezoelectric properties, while the Burgers-Faraday model represents a third-level complexity model of the same type. These three rheological models of higher complexity—in their classical linear forms—are already widely used; the author believes that the newly introduced fractional-type models (named by the author) will also see widespread application, initially in the validation of experimental research and subsequently in practical use. The lecturer also believes that these results open up new challenges regarding the development of software for calculating inverse Laplace transforms of complex Laplace-transformed expressions, thereby expanding the scope of artificial intelligence in areas where it is currently underdeveloped and limited.

This research explores secondary education teachers" perceptions regarding the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into instructional practice. Through semi-structured interviews with a sample of ten (10) educators from diverse academic backgrounds, the study examines three core pillars: interaction and usability, issues of trust and ethics, and the transformation of professional identity. The findings reveal that using AI tools is a complex cognitive process requiring strategic prompt engineering. Despite the small sample size, participants consistently demonstrated a "cautious acceptance," acting as critical evaluators of machine-generated outputs to mitigate scientific inaccuracies and "hallucinations." In conclusion, the study highlights a shift in the teaching role from being a source of knowledge to an authority of critical mediation. It emphasizes the urgent need for professional development that fosters pedagogical agency and ethical action within the modern digital learning environment.

documents.abstract: Abstract—As cellular architectures transition from 5G toward Sixth-Generation (6G) wireless networks, the classical Shannon-Nyquist paradigm of bit-level data transmission is rapidly approaching its theoretical physical channel capacity limits. Ultra-dense Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, autonomous vehicular swarms, and extended reality (XR) telepresence demand terabit-per-second (Tbps) data rates, sub-millisecond latencies, and continuous real-time edge artificial intelligence (AI) inference over severely bandwidth-constrained wireless channels. Classical communications optimize bit error rates (BER), transmitting massive streams of uncompressed binary representations regardless of the underlying computational task. Semantic Communications and Task-Oriented Edge Intelligence establish a transformative paradigm shift: shifting the transmission objective from error-free bit reconstruction to the faithful transmission of actionable semantic meaning and task-relevant latent features. By uniting Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC) with transformer-based feature extractors, semantic communication frameworks filter out redundant sensory data at the transmitter, communicating only task-critical representations to edge compute nodes. However, deploying semantic communications over stochastic wireless channels introduces acute foundational challenges: semantic noise induced by channel fading, joint training instability across non-differentiable wireless channels, and catastrophic performance degradation under out-of-distribution physical channel shifts. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of semantic communications for 6G edge intelligence. We formalize the rate-distortion-perception tradeoff under Weaver-Shannon semantic communication tiers, model continuous-time Deep JSCC over Rayleigh and Rician fading channels, and establish Lyapunov-guided end-to-end latency bounds for distributed edge inference. Furthermore, we construct an empirical software-defined radio (SDR) and GPU testbed evaluating multimodal perception and edge autonomous vehicle telemetry under severe signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) degradation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that Deep JSCC semantic transmission achieves a 78.4% reduction in required channel bandwidth while preserving 94.6% downstream edge classification accuracy under extreme channel noise (SNR = -6 dB), where classical JPEG/264 paired with LDPC coding completely collapses. Finally, we formulate open research directions in semantic knowledge base synchronization, neuro-symbolic semantic verification, and zero-trust semantic cybersecurity. Index Terms—Semantic Communications, 6G Wireless Networks, Edge Intelligence, Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (Deep JSCC), Task-Oriented Communications, Shannon-Weaver Levels, Physical Layer AI.

Abstract Prior research has shown that customers’ perceptions of chatbots may be influenced by the situational context in which human–chatbot interactions take place. This research advances understanding of artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled chatbot‐led service failure recovery (SFR) in the context of customer loyalty. Using a social constructivist philosophical perspective and an inductive approach, 52 in‐depth interviews were conducted to capture individuals’ perceptions of chatbot‐led interactions during a SFR process and how these perceptions impacted their trust in, and commitment to, brands. Utilizing commitment‐trust theory and trust transfer theory, we propose a framework that characterizes the relationships between a chatbot‐led SFR process and customer loyalty intentions. Based on the emergent data, customers’ evaluations of a service recovery journey led by chatbots can be grouped into four main outcomes: continued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand; continued trust in, and commitment to, brand; discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot; and discontinued trust in, and commitment to, chatbot and brand. Our findings extend current understanding of how consumers’ trust and commitment during chatbot‐led interactions during SFR evolve and highlight the dynamic relationship between consumers and the context of interactions. This study has theoretical and practical implications for developing and leveraging customers’ loyalty in AI‐enabled chatbot‐led SFR environments.

This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Statistical analyses (Welch's t test, Pearson's χ² test) revealed a digital privacy paradox: despite widespread endorsement of children's right to privacy, as many as 61.6% of parents of children aged 6–15 do not always ask their children for consent before publishing their image, or do not always respect their answers. This practice illustrates the discounting of the child's digital sovereignty from a paternalistic life position. Mothers were more likely than fathers to approach sharenting relationally, seeking digital strokes through the Child ego state. Higher self-assessed knowledge co-occurred with stronger concerns about artificial intelligence and with a propensity for corrective action (41.7% of parents had deleted previously posted photos of their child). The shift toward a position that recognizes the child as a subject occurs in response to adolescents' resistance or to parental self-reflection. The pedagogical implications point to the need for workshops on relational digital maturity and for promoting digital consent from the earliest years.

This article examines sharenting practices among parents in relation to the recognition of the child's agency and the underlying relational mechanisms, interpreted through the lens of Educational Transactional Analysis (ETA). The empirical study employed a questionnaire-based survey of N = 420 parents of children aged 6-15 attending primary schools in Poznań, Poland. Statistical analyses (Welch's t test, Pearson's χ² test) revealed a digital privacy paradox: despite widespread endorsement of children's right to privacy, as many as 61.6% of parents of children aged 6–15 do not always ask their children for consent before publishing their image, or do not always respect their answers. This practice illustrates the discounting of the child's digital sovereignty from a paternalistic life position. Mothers were more likely than fathers to approach sharenting relationally, seeking digital strokes through the Child ego state. Higher self-assessed knowledge co-occurred with stronger concerns about artificial intelligence and with a propensity for corrective action (41.7% of parents had deleted previously posted photos of their child). The shift toward a position that recognizes the child as a subject occurs in response to adolescents' resistance or to parental self-reflection. The pedagogical implications point to the need for workshops on relational digital maturity and for promoting digital consent from the earliest years.

Conversational Recommender Systems (CRSs) require reliable user simulators for cost-effective evaluation. LLM-based simulators have made realistic simulation possible but typically condition on profiles derived from explicit ratings, demographics, and static sources capturing surface preferences while omitting implicit behavioral characteristics such as decision-making style, aspect-level preferences, and domain expertise. We propose SimInter, a pipeline that elicits these attributes via synthetic interviews between two LLM agents, grounded in the user's statistical profile and historical conversational evidence. Before profile enrichment, an audit agent explicitly flags potential fabrication and stereotyping at the turn level. We instantiate and evaluate SimInter on movie recommendation. We simulate 300 ReDial users and, on a matched subset of 100 users, compare SimInter with a statistics-only baseline: SimInter significantly increases the diversity of expressed preference aspects (filtered aspect entropy: 1.619 vs. 0.859; paired d = 0.96, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). This gain persists when the simulator converses with two trained recommenders, KBRD and UniCRS, under two independent evaluation judges (+0.28 to +0.56 nats; all p < 0.001). Human evaluation finds 94.3% of enriched-attribute claims supported or partially supported, while human judgments agree with 95.2% of the auditor's binary filtering decisions on a stratified sample.

Background: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) requires a coordinated and effective response, with non-technical skills (NTS) playing an important role in patient safety. Deficiencies in these skills may contribute to preventable clinical errors. Objectives: To map the scientific evidence on the contribution of simulation to the development of NTS among healthcare teams in the context of CPR. Methods: This scoping review followed JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting recommendations. MEDLINE, CINAHL, Nursing & Allied Health Collection: Comprehensive and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched via EBSCOhost up to 7 July 2026. Eligibility followed Population, Concept and Context criteria; two reviewers independently selected and charted the evidence. Results: The 27 included sources yielded three themes: simulation as a strategy for skill development; NTS in CPR; and complementary educational interventions. Communication was the most frequently reported NTS, alongside leadership, teamwork, situational awareness, and decision-making. Reported improvements varied across sources and skills, and some diminished or were only partially retained over time. Debriefing was addressed in 21 sources (77.8%). Evidence on complementary technologies remained preliminary, with some tools lacking formal evaluation or validation. Conclusions: The findings provide a descriptive map of heterogeneous evidence and suggest that simulation may support NTS development, particularly with structured debriefing. They do not establish effectiveness or effects on clinical outcomes. Robust quantitative and longitudinal studies using validated measures are needed to confirm observed trends and assess retention, transfer to practice, team performance, patient safety, and clinical outcomes.

The study measurements of the human body are applied in various fields today, viz., ergonomics, kinanthropometry, medical purposes, fashion and merchandising, online retailing, and many more. As our lives have become fast-paced over time to get the clothing or accessory items made especially for an individual, the ready-to-wear industry expanded on the formula of standardising sizes and creating apparel in bulk. Although to consider that the human physique has a fixed set of sizes that progress and regress based on a mathematical formula is a faulty system in itself. In this chapter, the authors discuss the same and apprise the problems and the solutions in the field of advanced anthropometry.

Abstract: The workforce skill requirements across industries have been fundamentally redefined by the fast transition brought about by Industry 4.0 technologies, which include automation, big data analytics, artificial intelligence (AI), and cyber-physical systems. In order to address dynamic and technology-driven skill gaps, traditional role-based talent management approaches are becoming less and less effective. Continuous learning and ongoing education are emphasised as essential components in preparing employees to adapt to the shifting demands of the industry. This study looks at how upskilling and reskilling programs driven by AI may close skill gaps in the Industry 4.0 ecosystem to acquire the workforce ready for the future. Through the use of AI-enabled learning, ongoing competency development, and digital adaptability, the study creates a conceptual framework that connects skill-based talent management practices (an independent variable) with workforce agility and organisational success (dependent factors). In order to gather opinions from managers and workers in technology-intensive businesses, the study uses a quantitative research approach and standardised survey tools.AI integration in talent development procedures improves strategic workforce planning, decreases skill obsolescence, and promotes cultures of continuous learning.

Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and $τ^2$-Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a tool for information retrieval to a partner in conversation, advice, and emotional support. This integrative review examines whether that shift is reshaping friendship and other social bonds. Drawing on relationship science, human–machine communication research, surveys, experiments, longitudinal panels, randomized trials, and meta-analyses published through September 2026, including emerging evidence from Arab societies, the review develops the Responsiveness–Reciprocity Bridge Model to explain why conversational AI can relieve loneliness in the moment yet fail to build the relational capital that sustains people over time. A substantial minority of adolescents and young adults already turn to chatbots when they feel sad, anxious, or lonely, and short-term interactions with companion systems can reduce loneliness about as much as talking with another person, largely because users feel heard. These gains do not establish that synthetic ties can replace human friendship. Close relationships require mutual need, sacrifice, shared history, and practical solidarity that chatbots do not provide; in a randomized experiment, a human peer outperformed a highly supportive chatbot, and longitudinal and large-sample studies associate intensive, companionship-oriented use with greater loneliness and lower well-being. In Arab contexts, culturally aligned and human-guided digital tools show promise, but claims that AI is widely replacing traditional friends are not supported by comparable prevalence research. The central implication is balance: AI can widen access to support, but only if it is designed, governed, and used as a bridge to human relationships rather than as a substitute for them.

Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.

Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.

Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.

Purpose: This study aims to evaluate suitable foundation systems for a three-story building constructed on soft soil in the centre of Basra City, Iraq. The study assesses the structural response, bearing capacity, punching shear, and settlement behaviour of different foundation types to identify an appropriate and practical foundation solution. Design/Methodology/Approach: The structural analysis of the three-story building was performed using STAAD.Pro to determine the reactions at the building supports. Subsequently, SAFE was used to model and analyse different foundation systems, including isolated footings, strip footings, and mat foundations with and without beams. The foundation systems were evaluated based on punching shear and settlement criteria. Research Limitation: The study focuses on a three-story building and the specific soft-soil conditions of central Basra; therefore, the findings may not be directly applicable to buildings with significantly different heights or soil conditions. Findings: The results indicated that all investigated foundation systems satisfied the punching shear requirements. However, most isolated footings exceeded the permissible settlement limit of 25.4 mm. Although the strip footing remained within the allowable settlement limit, its application was considered impractical because of its limited economic feasibility and construction difficulties. The mat foundation modelled as a flat slab achieved a maximum settlement of 14 mm, while the mat foundation with beams recorded a maximum settlement of 19.8 mm. Practical Implication: The results indicate that mat foundations are suitable for low-rise buildings on soft soil. The mat foundation with beams provides a more economical alternative to the flat-slab mat foundation. Social Implication: Selecting an appropriate foundation system can improve building safety, reduce construction risks, and contribute to more reliable and sustainable urban development in areas characterised by soft soil. Originality/Value: This study compares foundation alternatives for low-rise buildings on soft soil in Basra, offering practical guidance for selecting safe and economically feasible foundation systems.

Generative AI has outpaced pedagogical and ethical guidance in accounting classrooms, leaving students and educators uncertain whether it supports or undermines the discipline's dual emphasis on procedural accuracy and professional judgment. To address this problem, this study examines how 92 business undergraduates perceive generative AI tools, notably ChatGPT, in accounting education, drawing on in-class, handwritten survey responses. Findings show that students view AI as a useful yet uncertain resource: valuing its speed, accessibility, and support while raising concerns over cheating, fairness, unclear institutional policies, and overreliance. Four interconnected themes emerged: Practical Affordances and Engagement, Ethical Tensions and Integrity, Curricular and Institutional Context, and Reflective Learning and Active Engagement. These results suggest student perceptions are shaped less by technology alone than by the pedagogical and ethical conditions of its introduction. Theoretically, the study identifies an augmentation–formation paradox specific to disciplines that combine codifiable procedure with professional judgment, which is advanced tentatively as extending the boundary conditions of paradox theory in education, a proposition that requires further empirical testing. Thematic analysis using a hybrid inductive–deductive coding strategy served as the primary analytic approach, supported by supplementary lexical analyses. The study contributes to management and accounting education by demonstrating that responsible AI integration requires clear guidance, reflective learning, and explicit alignment among AI use, assessment design, and academic integrity.

This paper starts from existing open-source weights, stacks new inference research on top of the optimization techniques already in use, and produces faster inference of the same model—without changing a single weight. Sushila.cpp is a free, local inference engine built on top of llama.cpp, the open-source engine behind Ollama, with SGLang on NVIDIA servers. Large language models are slow and expensive to run mainly because every generated token reads the model’s weights (for mixture-of-experts models, its active experts) from memory again. SUSHILA (Scalable Upstream Synthesis for Hybrid Inference in Large-model Acceleration) tests the published speed-up methods on each model once, right after its release, keeps those that make it faster at unchanged quality, and adds methods of our own. One of them, a landscape precomputed once per model, previews every next-token score cheaply, then computes only the best candidates exactly, reading 13–15% of the output layer with ≥99.75% agreement on the top token (7–70B models). Over eight GPU chat and coding models, Sushila.cpp achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 2.35× over Ollama (up to 4.05× on Llama-3.3-70B, on 160 benchmark prompts it never saw, with GSM8K accuracy unchanged within its error bars), measured on an NVIDIA A100 with Sushila.cpp’s SGLang serving path. Most of this gain comes from existing methods; our precomputed draft heads add 1–11% where a good head was already published and are most of the gain where none was: 3.64× on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and 3.56× on Kimi-Dev-72B. Speed tests were done on one NVIDIA A100 80GB for chat and coding models (media mostly on one RTX 4090; engine-level tests also on CPUs), one user at a time; results may vary on other computers. Every result has its scripts and raw outputs in our public repository, and each chat and coding comparison reruns with one command.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has established a new technological and organizational landscape across all industries, yet the process of creating AI architecture remains disjointed, intuitive, and domain-oriented. The proposed study introduces a System-Analytical Framework of Artificial Intelligence Architecture Design (SA-AI Framework), a collection of principles from systems analysis and multi-criteria decision-making intended to harmonize architectural design processes across heterogeneous AI domains. The paper is based on twenty-five current studies in explainable AI, neural-symbolic architectures, human-centered robotics, agentic systems, and domain-specific applications, such as healthcare, finance, energy, and education, that inform a comparative synthesis of architectural design principles. A Research Design Science Research (DSR) approach is used to model and test the SA-AI Framework conceptually across four stages: requirements analysis, identification of architectural alternatives, multi-criteria evaluation, and model validation. Results show that the framework offers a systematic, defensible method for constructing AI architectures, enabling greater exposure, flexibility, and decision-making effectiveness. It has cohesively unified the different models of AI, including the agentic AI, Explainable AI (XAI), Human-Centered AI (HCAI), and safety-driven architectures, providing both theory and practice to AI engineering and policy design. This paper concludes that system analysis helps design AI systems that integrate both technical and socio-technical systems to enhance the governance, reliability, and sustainability of intelligent architecture in the next generation.

The article examines the digitalization of education as a systemic transformation based on pedagogical objectives, management, competencies, and ethical principles. It explores contemporary digital education concepts and their relationship with pedagogical approaches and proposes an integrative model for educational institutions. The model promotes the pedagogically purposeful use of digital technologies while prioritizing the human factor and evidence-based decision-making.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a popular training paradigm for LLMs, providing dense, token-level supervision by aligning a model's own distribution with the distribution induced by privileged information. However, existing OPSD methods derive supervision solely from privileged information of the same instance, leaving inter-instance supervision largely unexplored. We propose Lookahead Self-Distillation (LEAD), which introduces inter-instance distillation by allowing the teacher to first learn from other on-policy rollouts before teaching the student. LEAD constructs lookahead teachers through virtual RL updates on disjoint subsets of on-policy rollouts, and uses each teacher to provide cross-group token-level supervision for the other subset. To reconcile the complementary yet potentially conflicting signals from OPSD and RLVR, we introduce harmonious modulation, which adaptively modulates the GRPO advantage based on the agreement between the two signals. Extensive experiments on scientific reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks show that LEAD achieves the best in-domain average performance across model scales while maintaining out-of-domain generalization comparable to GRPO.

Elementary students’ mathematics learning motivation declines systematically across early schooling and predicts subsequent academic achievement, yet no prior systematic review has integrated the instructional, relational, emotional, and epistemological dimensions of teacher influence within a single framework. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus on 30 March 2025 using a PEO-based Boolean strategy; 531 unique records were screened, yielding 16 included studies whose methodological quality was appraised using MMAT 2018 and synthesized through thematic narrative synthesis. Findings indicate that autonomy-supportive instruction and formative assessment enhance intrinsic motivation, positive teacher-student relationships correlate with motivation while conflict and dependency undermine it, teacher mindfulness programs yield modest but causally demonstrated effects, and inquiry-oriented epistemological beliefs indirectly raise student motivation through teacher efficacy. An integrated four-channel model of teacher influence is proposed, providing an evidence base for teacher professional development programs that simultaneously target instructional, relational, emotional, and epistemological competencies, particularly relevant to Indonesia’s Kurikulum Merdeka reform. Keywords: Elementary Education, Mathematics Learning Motivation, Self-Determination Theory, Systematic Literature Review, Teacher Factors

To read the full-text Open Access article and download the PDFs, please visit our Issue portal at Paradigm (Walter de Gruyter): https://reference-global.com/article/10.56508/mhgcj.v9i1.374 Introduction: Workplace mental health promotion in higher education requires attention to how digital technologies reshape teaching demands and resources. Purpose: To identify perceived demands and resources surrounding teacher-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) and interpret their implications for teachers’ mental health promotion. Methodology: An exploratory mixed-methods study combined a survey of 150 participants (56 English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers and 94 students/student-tutors) with 12 teacher interviews at two Ukrainian universities in January-February 2026. Descriptive statistics and four exploratory Fisher exact tests with Holm adjustment were integrated with thematic analysis of 30 selected translated interview extracts. Job Demands-Resources and self-determination theories informed a post-hoc interpretation. Results: Among teachers, 53.6% rated an AI platform for EFL teachers (Twee) very useful for preparation-time saving and 57.1% for task variety. Across the mixed sample, access (27.3%), quality assurance (22.0%), curriculum alignment (20.0%), and training/time (20.0%) were the leading constraints. Interview extracts linked anticipated workload relief to individual student support, while highlighting learning demands and the importance of professional judgment, empathy, and mentoring. Conclusions: These perceptions identify work-design issues relevant to mental health promotion during AI implementation. Participatory decisions, protected learning and recovery time, and accessible psychosocial support are priorities for institutional consideration

This thesis analyzes teachers’ pedagogical decision-making in selecting and adapting artificial intelligence-generated academic texts for Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT) in the context of teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) in Uzbekistan. The study considers texts generated by generative AI tools not as ready-to-use teaching materials, but as resources that require linguistic, content-related, and methodological evaluation and adaptation by teachers to suit specific learning tasks. Particular attention is paid to teachers’ decisions based on lexical and grammatical complexity, content accuracy and reliability, students’ language proficiency, the characteristics of academic discourse, the communicative purpose of the task, and relevance to the local educational context. The study also systematizes adaptation strategies such as simplifying and shortening texts, replacing lexical items, contextualizing content, and transforming texts into TBLT tasks. The analysis demonstrates that artificial intelligence does not automatically guarantee pedagogically appropriate materials and that the quality of the final learning materials depends on teachers’ professional judgment, linguistic competence, and methodological decisions.

Intensive English Programs have undergone major changes in how technology supports language education and research. At the University of Pittsburgh&s;s English Language Institute, early efforts centered on custom-built software that supported both classroom instruction and research, culminating in projects such as the PELIC corpus. Over time, however, there has been an industry-wide shift toward off-the-shelf platforms emphasizing usability and integration, often at the cost of research adaptability. Throughout these shifts, work in linguistics, applied linguistics, and related fields (such as second language studies, corpus linguistics, and psycholinguistics) have remained a key influence, and these areas have been strongly influenced by the scholarship of Alan Juffs. Looking ahead, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as large language models offer personalized learning opportunities but also pose risks. They challenge assumptions about the assessment of linguistic proficiency and complicate future research by undermining the provenance of learner-provided text.
