The PELIC corpus, completed under Juffs’ leadership just before the rise of GenAI, serves as a gift to future research, capturing robust learner data from the “pre-AI” era.

This study examines how pedagogical innovation can support Generation Z students in post-COVID marketing education, where hybrid learning and artificial intelligence are reshaping course design. It introduces the Pedagogical Innovation Pentagon, an evidence-informed model organized around five interrelated dimensions: hybridization, digitalization, artificial intelligence, responsibility, and harmonization. The model was developed and evaluated through a mixed-methods exploratory study conducted with first-year students enrolled in a bilingual introductory marketing course within a multi-campus business program. The model was implemented through an Instructional Capsule, a structured learning environment combining bilingual content development, guided activities, feedback mechanisms, sustainability-focused case studies, and shared assessment practices across campuses. Student self-reports and course analytics were used to explore how this instructional approach supported engagement, clarity, feedback, ethical awareness, and coherence in students’ learning experiences. Findings suggest that effective innovation in marketing education depends less on technological sophistication than on the meaningful integration of digital tools within a human-centered and ethically intentional learning environment. The study contributes to marketing education by offering a transferable approach for integrating digital transformation, AI, and responsible pedagogy into course design and continuous improvement.

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to personalize science instruction, yet evidence regarding teachers’ AI-supported practices and learners’ cognitive engagement remains limited. This study examined Grade 8 Science teachers’ practices embedded with AI-driven adaptive learning systems at Bongabon National High School, Nueva Ecija, during school year 2026–2027. Specifically, it described teachers’ profiles and practices across planning and preparation, classroom environment, instruction, and professional responsibilities, and investigated relationships and differences in respondents’ perceptions. A descriptive survey design with quasi-experimental designation, involved six Grade 8 Science teachers and 499 students. Teacher respondents were covered through complete enumeration, while student respondents were selected through simple random sampling. Questionnaires provided data analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t-tests, and Spearman’s rho. Findings indicated that AI-embedded teaching practices were “Always Practiced,” with an overall grand weighted mean of 3.60. Classroom environment obtained the highest combined domain mean (3.64), followed by instruction (3.62), planning and preparation (3.59), and professional responsibilities (3.55). Teachers’ educational attainment showed significant negative relationships with planning and preparation (rho = −0.892) and classroom environment (rho = −0.874), whereas other profile variables showed no significant relationships. Teachers’ and learners’ perceptions did not differ significantly across domains. The study concluded that AI-supported teaching practices were consistently reported and recommended targeted professional development and activities to strengthen comparatively less-practiced areas. These findings may guide context-responsive integration of adaptive learning tools in junior high school Science instruction while supporting reflective teaching practice and student engagement. This supports responsible implementation.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The transition toward Industry 5.0 promotes human-centred production systems in which digital technologies augment human capabilities rather than replace them. Within this paradigm, Digital Intelligent Assistants have emerged as promising tools to support operators during complex industrial tasks. Moreover, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including Large Language Models and Vision Language Models, enables the development of such systems by combining natural language interaction with visual perception. This exploratory mixed-methods pilot study investigates the impact of a multimodal Digital Intelligent Assistant (M-DIA) designed to support operators during a manual assembly process. A controlled laboratory experiment involving 60 participants compared four conditions: multimodal interaction (voice and camera), voice-only interaction, camera-only interaction, and a manual baseline. The analysis considered process performance, perceived cognitive workload, usability and user experience, and operator behaviour. The results show that M-DIA improves assembly quality by reducing product errors compared with the manual condition, although no reduction in total process time is observed due to interaction-related delays. From a human perspective, the assistant reduces perceived cognitive workload, while higher frustration levels emerge in configurations involving voice interaction. Usability and user experience evaluations are overall positive across all experimental conditions. Behavioural observations further indicate that operators maintain an active supervisory role, critically assessing system outputs and avoiding systematic overreliance on the assistant. These findings provide preliminary empirical evidence on the role of GenAI-based multimodal assistants in human-centred manufacturing and highlight key design implications for their industrial deployment.

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has introduced new paradigms for teaching, learning, and assessment, especially in the development of students’ writing performance. This meta-analysis examines the effectiveness of blended, technology-enhanced, and AI-supported instructional interventions on student learning outcomes. Eleven studies representing 477 participants across primary, secondary, and higher-education settings were synthesized. The included studies represented heterogeneous educational contexts and assessed outcomes such as academic achievement, literacy, vocabulary and language learning, digital literacy, and motivation. Accordingly, the pooled effect represents an overall effect on student learning outcomes rather than a writing-proficiency-specific effect. Studies were identified through ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and represented 477 participants across elementary, secondary, and higher-education settings and diverse disciplinary contexts. The results revealed a large and statistically significant pooled effect size [Hedges’ g = 0.89, 95% CI (0.76, 1.10)], showing that students who participated in technology-enhanced instructional interventions outperformed those receiving traditional instruction. Exploratory moderator analyses showed differences according to educational level, intervention duration, and technology type, with primary and secondary students, medium-length interventions (4–8 weeks), and interactive tools showing the strongest effects. The findings show the potential of thoughtfully integrated digital and AI-supported tools to enhance teaching and learning.

In this interview with Qiu Zeqi, professor at Peking University and internationally recognized intellectual, we explore aspects related to his academic trajectory and inquire about the complex relationship between technology and society, both in general and specifically in China. The focus of the questions lies within the field of Science and Technology Studies (STS) in China, addressing historical elements that shaped the foundations of Chinese society, as well as contemporary themes, challenges and their possible developments. Additionally, Professor Qiu offers thought-provoking reflections on Brazil-China relations across various sectors. The overarching objective is to understand these elements and their interplay with technology through an exploratory qualitative interview, drawing on the author’s articles and works. Thus, the interview contributes to a deeper comprehension of key themes in the STS field, recent processes of sociotechnical transformation in China, future perspectives associated with the evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies, and reflections for Brazil and Latin America. Keywords: Science, Technology and Society; Social Studies of Science and Technology; Artificial Intelligence; China; China-Brazil relations.
topics: Interdisciplinary Studies: Technology, Society, and Humanities
Science, Technology, and Education in Latin America

documents.abstract: Watermarking embeds an imperceptible signal in text from large language models that is statistically detectable with a secret key. The recent textGrain watermark (Li et. al. (2026b)) calibrates this signal against the model's sampling entropy through an explicit entropy budget, combining the stochasticity of Red-Green and the unbiasedness of Gumbel-max watermarks, and its accompanying report proposes a detector that sums pivotal statistics. We study when, and how efficiently, textGrain can be detected after human edits, modeled as a sparse mixture in which a fraction $\varepsilon_n\asymp n^{-p}$ of positions retain the watermark and token uncertainty decays as $n^{-q}$. First, entropy calibration comes at a cost: the minimax detection boundary of textGrain is $p+q=1/2$, so its detectable region is strictly smaller than that of Gumbel-max and maximal-coupling watermarks, whose boundary is $2p+q=1$. This cost stems from textGrain's construction rather than from entropy calibration itself: an unbiased scheme with the same entropy loss remains detectable where textGrain is not. Second, perhaps surprisingly, this loss makes the sum detector optimal at the boundary when the number of transport columns is fixed, unlike for Gumbel-max. When the number of columns grows and the entropy budget does not vanish, the detectable region expands while that of the sum detector does not. Third, for a fixed edit fraction, we characterize the optimal exponential rate of type II error decay and show that the sum detector falls strictly short of it at every fixed alternative. Finally, we propose a weighted multiscale binomial scan, valid in finite samples and needing no knowledge of the next-token distributions, entropy budget, or edit fraction; it attains every detection boundary above and the optimal exponent.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled across groups, including observations that yield no proposed edit, to refine their content and applicability. Reviewed proposals form a bounded textual patch, with adoption of the candidate context determined by held-out validation rewards. Together, these components establish a reward-driven policy optimization loop in which multiple attempts jointly inform reusable context updates. We evaluate TextualRL with five target agents on six benchmarks. Averaged over the six benchmarks, TextualRL improves test accuracy over the base model by 24.4 and 15.3 percentage points for GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.8-27B, respectively.

This study investigates the psychological mechanisms through which artificial intelligence (AI) literacy relates to L2 learners’ willingness to write (WTW). It proposes a serial mediation model wherein L2 writing self-efficacy (WSE) and L2 writing anxiety (WA) sequentially mediate this relationship. Grounded in social cognitive theory and control-value theory, the research employed a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design with 303 Chinese EFL learners. Quantitative results from structural equation modeling indicate that: (1) L2 WSE fully mediates the relationship between AI literacy and L2 WTW; (2) AI literacy is indirectly linked to L2 WTW through a sequential pathway: by first positively predicting L2 WSE, which in turn negatively predicts L2 WA; and (3) the direct effects of AI literacy on L2 WA and L2 WTW are non-significant. To explain these quantitative pathways, qualitative interviews with 16 participants further elucidated how AI tool usage corresponds to higher L2 WSE through strategic partnership, reduced startup burden, and task scaffolding support. Furthermore, the qualitative narratives revealed that while AI usage can initially be associated with anxiety (e.g., fear of exposure, tool-related frustration), the heightened L2 WSE linked to AI literacy effectively serves as a protective factor against these affective barriers. The study concludes that AI literacy positively correlates with L2 WTW through a fully indirect mechanism, in which heightened L2 WSE serves as a vital prerequisite for lowering L2 WA. These findings contribute to theory by integrating two major psychological frameworks and offer practical implications for leveraging AI to cultivate more willing L2 writers.

Digitalization is transforming the workplace and the way of doing business in various sectors.Industry 4.0, commonly known as the fourth industrial revolution, has changed the way people work, develop, manage, control, hire and interact with each other.Indeed, we are witnessing a change in the nature of jobs.Today, muscle jobs are disappearing and brain jobs are growing, and labor-based industries are coming from skill-based industries and will have to be replaced by knowledge-based industries.In this extremely aggressive situation where everyone interacts with each other, technology and innovation are transforming the world into a global village worldwide.Artificial intelligence helps companies perform any function more effectively and efficiently.The purpose of this research is to conduct a bibliometric analysis of the scientific literature that addresses the application and impact of artificial intelligence in the field of human resource management in a connected way.At the same time the topic is quite new and this paper will contribute to scientific researches in the form of theoretical background.In the article literature review related to the topic will be used.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In 2016, a leading AI researcher predicted that machine learning would render radiologists obsolete within five years. A decade later, the opposite has happened. Radiology is among the most competitive specialties in medicine, and artificial intelligence has become a tool that makes physicians faster, more accurate, and more capable rather than a force that replaces them. This chapter traces that shift across radiology, pathology, ophthalmology, cardiology, and stroke and diabetic eye care, where AI now detects disease, triages urgent cases, and extends screening to populations that were previously underserved. The recurring lesson is that augmentation, not automation, defines AI’s clinical value, and that its safe and effective use depends on physicians who understand both its capabilities and its limits. By establishing this framing, the chapter sets up the practical questions the rest of the book addresses: how to evaluate AI tools, integrate them into clinical workflows, navigate the ethical challenges they raise, and redefine physician expertise for a new era of medicine.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The dominance of Euro-American frameworks in industrial and organizational psychology has rendered culturally embedded work experiences largely invisible. While foundational models such as the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework elegantly illuminate universal engagement mechanisms across diverse contexts, occupational health literature has traditionally paid less attention to how intersecting racialized and gendered identities shape occupational well-being in postcolonial settings. This conceptual paper addresses this contextual gap by examining the organizational position of Black women in South African middle management, a group navigating unique structural tensions rooted in historical exclusion and contemporary marginalization. Responding to calls for disciplinary decolonization, I propose an integrated Afrocentric framework that brings Bosadi theorization into conversation with salutogenic principles. Specifically, I argue that Bosadi identity functions are not merely as a demographic marker but as a culturally embedded personal resource that shapes how job demands are interpreted, managed, and made meaningful. By positioning identity as an analytic resource rather than a contextual variable, the framework extends the JD-R model’s explanatory power to account for culturally specific modes of resilience and meaning-making. The paper concludes by outlining theoretical contributions to organizational psychology and offering directions for empirical research, including methodological considerations for studying culturally situated work experiences. This work aims to support the development of organizational practices that are genuinely responsive to the lived realities of historically marginalized women.

This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

The pressure to implement formative evaluation of English in colleges and universities is increasing day by day, and the massive and complex learning data increases the burden of teachers' evaluation. Artificial intelligence can run through the whole evaluation process, improve evaluation efficiency, and promote the transformation of digital teaching for teachers. This paper takes college English teachers as the object, relies on multi-source data to build an analysis framework, and explores the relationship between AI-empowered formative evaluation and teachers' digital competence. The research shows that teachers' AI application has the characteristics of staged evolution, digital ability differentiates with the degree of AI integration, and the overall competency improvement effect is obviously stratified. This study improves the relevant theoretical system, and also provides practical reference for teacher training, intelligent teaching platform optimization and evaluation reform. AI has become a key boost to reshape the evaluation model and enhance teachers' digital literacy.

This article critically examined the Eames DSS Stacking chair (1950) as a paradigmatic case of the tensions between the democratization of modern design and the logics of industrial capitalism. The central problem lay in the contradiction between its emancipatory promise — making functional and aesthetic design accessible to the masses — and its entanglement in the standardization, pseudo-individualization, and commodification dynamics characteristic of the Culture Industry. Using a qualitative case-study approach, the research applied a theoretical triangulation combining Adorno and Horkheimer’s theory, Benjamin’s reflections on technical reproducibility, and Llovet’s semiotics of value as reinterpreted by Anderson and Girod. The analysis revealed that, while the chair achieved a massive distribution exceeding 20 million units and represented a significant ergonomic breakthrough, it simultaneously sacrificed artisanal singularity, subordinated use-value to capitalist exchange-value, and reproduced ideological mechanisms of cultural control. The research further showed that the chair’s contemporary reception in institutions such as MoMA demonstrates capitalism’s capacity to absorb and recycle its own critiques, transforming objects with a democratizing vocation into icons of cultural distinction. The study concludes that any genuinely democratizing design proposal must confront these structural contradictions rather than merely celebrating technical efficiency or superficial accessibility.

This chapter examines how circular economy (CE) imaginaries are articulated and stabilised within the fashion industry. Drawing on the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, it analyses the Global Fashion Summit 2025 as a field-configuring event where competing visions of circular transition are publicly performed. Based on participant observation, session recordings, and field notes, the study identifies five distinct CE imaginaries. The findings show that these imaginaries stabilise unevenly through discourses, representations, institutions, and identities, shaping how circularity becomes actionable. The chapter contributes to fashion business and management research by demonstrating that CE transition is not governed by a single coherent pathway, but constructed through multiple co-existing visions that prioritise different problems, solutions, and actors.

Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstract. The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, particularly in the development of speaking proficiency. AI-powered chatbots, speech recognition systems, conversational agents, and generative AI applications enable learners to practise English, receive immediate feedback, and engage in interactive communication beyond the traditional classroom. This article examines the potential impact of AI-assisted learning on EFL learners’ speaking proficiency, with particular attention to the educational context of Uzbek universities. It explores the ways in which AI-based tools may support speaking fluency, pronunciation, grammatical accuracy, vocabulary development, learner confidence, and willingness to communicate. Drawing on existing research and pedagogical perspectives, the article discusses the opportunities and limitations of integrating AI into higher education. Particular attention is given to speaking anxiety, unequal access to digital resources, feedback reliability, learner autonomy, and the importance of teacher guidance. The analysis suggests that AI can serve as a valuable supplementary resource when integrated into structured pedagogical activities. However, its effectiveness depends on learners’ engagement, instructional design, and the combination of technological practice with authentic human interaction. Further empirical research involving Uzbek university students is necessary to establish the extent and long-term effects of AI-assisted speaking instruction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, EFL learners, speaking proficiency, AI-assisted learning, university students, conversational AI, language anxiety, Uzbekistan, digital education.

The fast growth of surveillance technology has drastically changed India's balance amongst individual liberty and political authority.Inconceivable amounts of data collection and behaviors analysis have been made possible by the combination of electronic tracking systems, AI (artificial intelligence), and sophisticated analysis of data.Although the legal framework created following the Apex Court's landmark decision in Honorable K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India recognized privacy or as essential rights (Fundamental right) within Article 21, it is still mostly restricted to the instructive and corporeal dimensions of confidentiality 1 .This study explores the idea of the "monitoring of thinking," which refers to electronically facilitated methods that use data trends and electronic (digital) behavioral assessment to infer, anticipate, and possibly affect humans thinking.Intellectual observation works by creating mental profiling and prediction models that disclose opinions, choices, and desires, in contrast with conventional observation, which concentrates on tracking activities or telecommunications .2Substantial constitutional issues are raised by such activities, especially in relation to liberty of expressing itself, psychological independence, and decency.The danger is increased by the potential for cognitive regulation and computational tampering which could stifle independent thinking and participatory engagement.The article makes the case that supreme law (Constitutional law) has a "silent blind zone" because it does not identify and control incursions into the intellectual realm.Judicial and parliamentary advances have not specifically tackled intellectual freedom or mental confidentiality, notwithstanding Puttaswamy expansive concept of confidentiality.This study shows that current statutory safeguards are inadequate to adequately safeguard people from the growing risks of mental monitoring via conceptual study and involvement with modern technical circumstances.3 As reaction, the article argues that Art.21 of Constitution should recognize a fresh basic entitlement (Right) to mental confidentiality or intellectual autonomy.In order to prevent advances in technology from undermining the fundamental principles of liberty, integrity, and democratization, it closes by highlighting the necessity of focused parliamentary improvements, judiciary creativity, and strong organizational safeguarding.

Work stress is a common occupational health problem among teachers and may affect psychological well-being and the quality of teaching. One factor suspected to be associated with work stress is job satisfaction. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between job satisfaction and work stress among teachers at SMP Negeri 14 and SMP Negeri 18, South Tangerang City. This study employed a quantitative design with a cross-sectional approach. The study population consisted of 96 active teachers from both schools, with 93 teachers meeting the study criteria and participating through total sampling. Data were collected using a respondent characteristics questionnaire, the Job Satisfaction Survey (JSS) to measure job satisfaction, and the Job Stress Scale to measure work stress. Data analysis included univariate and bivariate analyses using the Chi-Square test at a 95% significance level. The results showed that 39.8% of respondents had low job satisfaction, 25.8% were categorized as ambivalent, and 34.4% had high job satisfaction. Most respondents (65.6%) experienced low work stress, while 34.4% experienced high work stress. Bivariate analysis revealed a significant relationship between job satisfaction and work stress (p < 0.001; OR = 8.27; 95% CI: 3.06–22.39), indicating that teachers with low job satisfaction had a higher risk of experiencing work stress than those with high job satisfaction. In addition, age, gender, and teaching workload were significantly associated with work stress. The study concludes that improving job satisfaction through improvements in the work environment, reward systems, organizational communication, and workload management is an important strategy for reducing work stress and enhancing teachers’ well-being.

This paper critically examines the persistent responsibility gap in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), arguing that current approaches fail to adequately bridge it. While XAI is often promoted as a remedy for the opacity of AI systems—the so-called “black box problem”—and as a way to enable human accountability in both high- and low-stakes AI applications, I contend that these hopes are premature. The paper distinguishes between legal and moral responsibility, arguing that regulation alone cannot address the full spectrum of responsibility gaps, especially in everyday, low-stakes scenarios. Then, I argue that XAI needs to tackle two separate but interconnected problems in its attempt to bridge the responsibility gap: an epistemological problem concerning the nature of XAI explanations, and a moral attribution problem regarding the distribution of blame and praise in situations where AI is involved in decision-making. Through detailed discussion of XAI methods and their limitations, I demonstrate that existing techniques often provide only post-hoc, technically focused explanations, which are insufficient for grounding moral responsibility. The paper concludes that without fundamental advances in both the design of explanations and our practices of responsibility attribution, the responsibility gap in AI will remain an unresolved and pressing issue for the field.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The awareness and perspectives of Scandinavian optometrists regarding artificial intelligence (AI) in eye care was evaluated through a web-based questionnaire. Responses from 421 optometrists were analyzed for familiarity, perceived benefits, concerns, and willingness to engage with AI technologies. Most participants expressed familiarity with AI and support for its inclusion in education and practice, though concerns regarding diagnostic accuracy and potential impacts on the patient-optometrist relationship were noted. These findings are critical for informing educational strategies and facilitating knowledge exchange aimed at addressing uncertainties and optimising the benefits of AI in eye care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to urban flood-risk reduction, with particular emphasis on data-driven forecasting, real-time monitoring, infrastructure management, emergency response, recovery, and resilient urban planning. AI technologies—including machine learning, predictive analytics, remote sensing, Internet of Things (IoT) networks, natural language processing, and image analysis—can support more accurate flood prediction, dynamic risk assessment, optimized drainage operations, and timely public communication. The paper also discusses the integration of AI into smart-city frameworks, the limitations of conventional flood-management approaches, challenges associated with data quality and availability, computational requirements, ethical considerations, and the need for interdisciplinary collaboration. In addition, an embedding-based long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture is presented for probabilistic streamflow forecasting in settings in which individual weather products may be unavailable. However, effective implementation requires robust data infrastructures, transparent model-development practices, appropriate institutional capacity, and supportive policy frameworks.

Abstract Motivation is central to successful English language learning because it influences effort, persistence, participation, and willingness to communicate. This thesis examines how gamification can support student motivation through a literature-based analysis of recent research. It argues that selected game elements may increase engagement when they promote competence, autonomy, meaningful progress, and social interaction. However, gamification is not automatically effective. Its value depends on careful alignment with language objectives, learner needs, and balanced classroom implementation. Keywords: EFL learners, engagement, gamification, intrinsic motivation, language learning, student motivation, willingness to communicate

Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

This dissertation investigates the displacement of human actors by generative AI performers in the fastest-growing segment of the screen entertainment economy: the vertical drama, or micro-drama, industry. The study is organized around a triggering case widely reported in October 2026, in which a nineteen-year-old actress, Hannah Lowery, was reportedly recast out of an ice-skating-themed series when the production shifted entirely to AI-generated performers. Using the video report as an entry point, the dissertation triangulates its claims against primary trade reporting, including Business Insider (June 2026), trade publications such as Variety, Mashable, and The Economic Times, regulatory documents, and a broad interdisciplinary literature spanning cultural economics, labor sociology, media theory, and machine learning. Methodologically, the dissertation combines (i) documentary and content analysis of the video case and its verification status, examining each claim individually; (ii) economic analysis of production cost structures, drawing on reported estimates of US$1,000–US$3,000 per AI-generated episode compared with US$100,000–US$300,000 for equivalent productions featuring human casts; (iii) institutional analysis of the emerging regulatory landscape, including the 2023 SAG-AFTRA agreements, California Assembly Bill 2602 (AB 2602), Tennessee’s ELVIS Act, the proposed federal NO FAKES Act, the European Union’s AI Act, and China’s provisions governing deep synthesis and generative AI; and (iv) the construction of forward-looking scenarios for the coming decade. The central argument is threefold. First, vertical dramas constitute a genuine entry-level market for synthetic performance in a manner consistent with disruption theory: their economics are driven by cost minimization and production volume rather than the premium emotional differentiation characteristic of high-end productions. Second, the displacement pressure documented in 2026 is driven less by audience preferences than by production-cost arbitrage and platformization dynamics. Survey evidence indicates that Western audiences still overwhelmingly prefer human stars, whereas Chinese production has already shifted substantially toward AI-generated content. Third, the emerging legal and ethical framework—encompassing consent, compensation, disclosure, and posthumous rights—will determine whether the industry converges toward regulated coexistence or experiences a cascade of substitutions with severe consequences for the talent pipeline. The dissertation contributes a verified factual foundation, a production cost-structure model, a four-scenario matrix, and a policy agenda for performers, producers, platforms, and regulators. Approximate main-text word count: 31,000.Figures: 7.Tables: 9.

Avian influenza A(H5N1) remains a major zoonotic and pandemic concern because of its extensive circulation in birds, repeated spillover into mammals, and capacity to cause illness in humans ranging from asymptomatic infection or conjunctivitis to fatal pneumonia. The detection of clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 in United States dairy cattle in 2024 created a persistent animal-human interface that required coordinated action across public health, animal health, occupational health, agriculture, and food safety. This review critically examines the role of the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in H5N1 surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, genomic risk assessment, clinical guidance, occupational protection, communication, and pandemic preparedness. A structured narrative review was conducted using PubMed and authoritative sources from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), World Health Organization (WHO), Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The search covered January 1996 through 24 July 2026. Sources were screened for direct relevance and synthesized by predefined thematic domains. Table 1 presents a focused evidence map of key H5N1-specific studies and reports. The CDC response uses surveillance systems, monitoring of exposed persons, public-health laboratory testing, rapid H5 subtyping, sequencing, antigenic characterization, and antiviral-susceptibility assessment. Human infections associated with the United States cattle and poultry outbreaks were predominantly mild and commonly involved conjunctivitis or upper-respiratory symptoms, although severe and fatal disease occurred. Preventive measures include occupational PPE guidance, monitoring and testing of exposed persons, infection-control recommendations, risk communication, and antiviral prophylaxis following selected high-risk exposures.” Important limitations include uneven testing, incomplete participation by exposed workers, barriers to personal protective equipment use, rapidly changing surveillance data, and uncertainty regarding the frequency of mild or asymptomatic infection. The reviewed serosurveys also indicated that symptom-based surveillance can miss infections in exposed workers. The CDC-centered response has expanded detection and preparedness, but its effectiveness depends on sustained One Health coordination, timely animal-outbreak control, accessible worker-centered testing, transparent data sharing, and continuous evaluation of viral evolution, diagnostic performance, antiviral susceptibility, and candidate vaccine-virus match and the need for stronger integration of animal and human data.

This study aims to describe the use of English songs as learning media and to analyze their role in increasing students’ motivation to learn English at SMP Alfaqih Muqaddam Kubu Raya. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed, involving 20 eighth-grade students and one English teacher as an informant. The songs used in the learning activities were Let It Go and Heal the World. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, questionnaires, and documentation, and were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings indicate that the use of English songs created a more engaging learning environment and encouraged students’ active participation. Observation results showed that 90% of the students were willing to repeat and practice the lyrics, 85% demonstrated enthusiasm during the learning process, and 80% paid attention while listening to the songs. Questionnaire results also revealed a high level of motivation, with an average score of 4.25 for the statement regarding increased motivation to learn English through songs. In addition to enhancing motivation, songs helped students retain vocabulary, improve pronunciation, build confidence, and experience a more enjoyable learning atmosphere. Let It Go particularly encouraged students’ confidence and courage, while Heal the World provided meaningful messages that supported intrinsic motivation. Despite several challenges, including difficulty understanding certain lyrics, pronunciation problems, and shyness when singing, these difficulties could be minimized through teacher guidance and repeated practice. Therefore, English songs can serve as practical, engaging, and effective learning media for supporting students’ motivation in learning English.

Abstract Research Summary We propose that entrepreneurship and strategy research can develop theory about phenomena of the future rather than only explain those of the past. Research has potential for practical relevance when researchers make claims towards applications to decisions practitioners have yet to make. Theory grounded in a world that may differ from the observed world can be built through a process of extrapolation from technological trends, a practice utilized by entrepreneurs and science fiction authors alike. Assuming advances in artificial intelligence, we apply this process to three emerging phenomena: governing scarcity in metaverse virtual worlds, redesigning organizations around pervasive monitoring via wearable devices, and allocating the intellectual property rights of humanoid robots. We argue that embracing theory that speaks to the future can enhance the practical and educational relevance of management research. Managerial Summary Assuming artificial intelligence continues to improve, we highlight three impending phenomena poised to transform conventional approaches to entrepreneurship and strategy. First, in metaverse virtual worlds, managers must manage resources governed by artificial scarcity. Second, with wearable devices allowing continuous monitoring, managers must consider alternative structures for vertical hierarchy and horizontal collaboration. Third, deployment of humanoid robots will complicate intellectual property rights and asset ownership. We propose that scholarship towards developing theoretical frameworks addressing these and other phenomena of the future will be relevant to both managers and students.

The development of artificial intelligence is predominantly assessed in terms of increasing cognitive performance. Yet this comparison presupposes a yardstick that captures the diversity of possible forms of intelligence only incompletely. The Theory of Attractor Horizons advances the thesis that intelligent systems, by virtue of their respective organization, can reach different regions of cognitive attractors that may partly overlap without being wholly contained within one another. Greater performance within one organizational form does not confer general access to the organizational possibilities of other forms. The theory explains this asymmetry through the dependence of reachable attractors on available transformation pathways and examines aggregation as a mechanism that can give rise to new organizational forms while also restricting existing possibilities. From this follows the far-reaching prediction that artificial systems will develop structures of thought whose internal organization the human brain cannot itself instantiate within its biological form of intelligence, even where individual results remain verifiable or technically useful. Conversely, human organizational attractors may exist that remain inaccessible to artificial systems despite their superior cognitive performance. For alignment, this entails limits to understanding-based oversight and requirements for verifiable coexistence between different forms of intelligence.

Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Islamic education requires a pedagogical model that preserves teachers’ epistemic authority while addressing adolescents’ health needs. This study examines the implementation, pedagogical affordances, and limitations of ChatGPT-assisted Fiqh al-Ṭahārah learning and develops a model for strengthening Islamic value-based reproductive health literacy. Employing a qualitative single-case study design, the research was conducted at MA Al Ishlah Banjarejo Blora. Data were collected through observations, semi-structured interviews, documentation, and analysis of students’ interactions with ChatGPT, and were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings revealed three stages of implementation: preparation, inquiry-based interaction, and reflection and verification. ChatGPT provided a psychologically safer space for sensitive questions, flexible access to explanations, contextualized Fiqh learning, increased engagement, and critical AI literacy. However, its use was constrained by potential inaccuracies, oversimplification of differences among Islamic legal schools, prompt quality, unequal access, and privacy and ethical concerns. The resulting AI-Assisted Thaharah Learning Model integrates AI-assisted inquiry, teacher facilitation, source verification, and Islamic value internalization while maintaining teachers’ pedagogical, epistemic, and moral authority.

Human–computer interaction (HCI) has traditionally relied on assumptions of a relatively uniform user. Neurodiversity challenges this premise by highlighting variation in perception, attention, communication, and sensory processing. Advances in multimodal sensing, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive interfaces increasingly enable systems to respond to changing user needs in real time. This paper proposes an evidence-informed taxonomy for empathic adaptive interaction design, developed through a structured interdisciplinary review and conceptual synthesis. The taxonomy comprises six dimensions: User Cognitive Profile, Empathic Inference Capability, Sensing Modality, Adaptation Strategy, Application Context, and Governance, Autonomy, and Ethics. Together, these dimensions provide a structured framework for analyzing how systems sense user state, infer support needs, adapt interaction, and maintain transparency and user control. The framework supports the systematic analysis, comparison, design, evaluation, and future empirical validation of inclusive, neuroadaptive, and multimodal interaction systems responsive to cognitive diversity.

Advances in multimodal sensing, artificial intelligence (AI), and adaptive interfaces increasingly enable systems to respond to changing user needs in real time. This paper proposes an evidence-informed taxonomy for empathic adaptive interaction design, developed through a structured interdisciplinary review and conceptual synthesis. The taxonomy comprises six dimensions: User Cognitive Profile, Empathic Inference Capability, Sensing Modality, Adaptation Strategy, Application Context, and Governance, Autonomy, and Ethics. Together, these dimensions provide a structured framework for analyzing how systems sense user state, infer support needs, adapt interaction, and maintain transparency and user control. The framework supports the systematic analysis, comparison, design, evaluation, and future empirical validation of inclusive, neuroadaptive, and multimodal interaction systems responsive to cognitive diversity.

Abstract Generative AI is likely to transform terminology work by creating new opportunities for automation. At the same time, it raises concerns about the future of terminologists and terminological resources, as efficiency pressures may encourage excessive automation based on the perception that human expertise can be replaced by AI. However, large language models remain unreliable for terminological purposes due to errors, hallucinations, and various forms of bias, making terminologists indispensable for ensuring the accuracy and reliability of terminological data. This paper argues that human-centered AI, an approach that emphasizes that AI’s primary goal should be to contribute to human well-being, provides a framework for maximizing the benefits of generative AI while mitigating its risks. It contends that high levels of automation and meaningful human control are compatible and desirable, and that AI should enhance terminologists’ capabilities while preserving their agency and decision-making authority. The implications of AI-assisted terminology work are examined through three interrelated dimensions: the augmented terminologist, ethical AI, and human-centered design. In particular, the paper addresses how AI integration reshapes the role of the terminologist, affects professional values and working conditions, requires the management of AI-generated bias, and calls for the design of AI tools around the terminologist’s needs. The paper concludes that a human-centered orientation is necessary to ensure that AI strengthens, rather than undermines, the essential role of terminology work in supporting specialized communication and the accurate transmission of knowledge across languages and cultures.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

Clinical communication is a fundamental skill that impacts patient satisfaction, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. Traditional training methods, such as standardized patients (SPs) or virtual standardized patients (VSPs), face barriers including high costs, logistical complexity, and lack of spontaneous interaction. This study addresses these challenges by developing a scalable alternative based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to train medical students in the anamnesis phase. We developed an interactive Conversational Virtual Patient (CVP) system, understood here as a text- and voice-based simulated patient without graphical embodiment. The conversational logic is orchestrated as an explicit state machine over the interview, implemented with LangGraph, a graph-based framework in which each node performs one processing stage and a shared state persists across turns. Clinical consistency across the interview is maintained by a semantic memory layer implemented with LangMem, a library that stores clinical facts as vector embeddings and retrieves them by similarity. Performance is measured by an automatic evaluation module assessing 24 communication criteria derived from validated instruments such as the Communication Assessment Tool (CAT) and the Communication Skills Scale (CSS). The platform was validated with 21 participants, comprising 9 eighth-semester medical students, 11 practising physicians, and 1 expert in healthcare technology. All sessions were conducted in Spanish. Considering the student cohort, which addresses the educational utility of the tool, the system obtained a Chatbot Usability Questionnaire (CUQ) score of 82.3/100 and an average acceptance of the automated feedback of 4.50/5. The physician and expert cohort, which provides expert clinical validation, obtained 96.5/100 and 4.21/5 respectively, yielding a pooled usability score of 90.4/100 and a pooled feedback acceptance of 4.33/5. In an exploratory comparison against eleven physician ratings of the same interviews, rank agreement was highest for “Interest” ( $$\rho = 0.64$$ ) and lowest for “Completeness” ( $$\rho = 0.09$$ ), and the automated scores fell below the physician scores in every dimension. No dimension attained significance after correction for six comparisons, and the confidence intervals were wide, so these coefficients describe the observed sample rather than the agreement attainable in general. The results support the feasibility of the system as a complement to traditional medical training, providing immediate and standardized feedback. Given the sample size and the single-institution design, these findings should be read as an initial validation of feasibility and acceptability rather than as evidence of pedagogical efficacy.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.

The detection of fake news and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated synthetic content has become one of the central challenges of contemporary information science. While deep learning approaches—particularly transformer-based language models and convolutional networks—have achieved strong performance on established benchmarks, their reliance on centralised training pipelines renders them ill-suited to the institutional, regulatory, and adversarial realities of real-world deployment. Simultaneously, the emergence of AI content watermarking as a regulatory instrument—culminating in the EU AI Act Article 50 Code of Practice published in December 2025—establishes a new technical landscape in which provenance signals should be primary rather than supplementary detection inputs. This chapter examines the convergence of three paradigms that together address the principal limitations of existing detection approaches: Federated Learning (FL), which enables privacy-preserving collaborative model training across distributed institutional participants without raw data exchange; blockchain technology, which provides verifiable, tamper-proof aggregation and audit infrastructure replacing the trusted central server assumption inherent in conventional FL; and multi-layer AI watermark verification, which integrates Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) Content Credentials, neural watermarking schemes such as Google SynthID, and cryptographic embedding approaches such as MetaSeal as first-class classification signals alongside content-based behavioural features. We systematically survey the state of the art across these three domains, analyse their theoretical and practical complementarities, and propose a unified architectural design that jointly addresses privacy preservation, Byzantine resilience, and standards-compliant provenance verification. A comprehensive compliance analysis against the EU AI Act Article 50 Code of Practice demonstrates that the proposed design satisfies all applicable technical obligations ahead of the August 2026 enforcement deadline. We further discuss the fundamental limitations and open research problems at the intersection of these paradigms, including the watermark trilemma, GDPR tensions with blockchain immutability, and the detection gap for unmarked synthetic content.

Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) enable diverse whole-body control, but adapting a pretrained controller to a new embodiment remains challenging because of kinematic and dynamic mismatch. We present TRACE, a framework for efficient cross-embodiment adaptation that preserves pretrained motion representations while specializing feedback control to the target robot.TRACE first injects kinematic priors into input and output projection layers and aligns nominal joint dynamics to reduce embodiment mismatch and support stable fine-tuning. It then combines encoder distillation with low-rank reinforcement learning on a compact, quality-screened motion set, using a two-phase curriculum to establish stable tracking before refining difficult motions. We apply TRACE to transfer SONIC from Unitree G1 to Unitree H2 using 10 million motion frames and approximately eight hours of training on a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU, at less than 0.1% of the GPU-hour cost of training SONIC from scratch. The adapted controller achieves 96.08\% success on 67,953 evaluation motions under a height-scaled tracking criterion. Real-robot demonstrations span dynamic motion tracking and whole-body teleoperation, with collected demonstrations supporting downstream vision-language-action policy post-training. These results demonstrate practical reuse of a pretrained humanoid controller across robots with different body scales and dynamics.

Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, yet remain susceptible to hallucination. Activation steering offers a promising mitigation approach by guiding parallel token predictions through internal representations. However, existing steering methods largely overlook two characteristics of dLLMs: dynamic denoising states and temporal hallucination risks, which challenge predefined steering vectors and uniform intervention strengths. We propose TRACESTEER, a trace-driven activation steering framework that uses preceding denoising predictions as feedback to jointly adapt steering direction and strength. Specifically, Denoising Feedback Steering (DF-Steering) constructs step-specific steering vectors from preceding predictions and current hidden states. Trajectory-Guided Steering Gate (TS-Gate) regulates their strength using prediction uncertainty and the denoising timestep. With the backbone frozen, factual supervision and magnitude regularization jointly guide the learning of adaptive steering interventions, promoting factual reliability and stability throughout denoising. Experiments on two dLLMs show improved factual reliability on TruthfulQA and generalization across five downstream benchmarks.

An edge server and nearby devices can train language models of different sizes together by mutual distillation. Federated unlearning (FU) and unlearning for large language models (LLMs) execute a removal request on one model. Under mutual distillation, however, the effect of the removed data has been copied into many students, and their uploads teach it back to the corrected teacher. We propose Holder-level Erasure via Replication-weighted Delta-closure (HERD), which decides which holders must be corrected. HERD records a knowledge lineage graph from the transfers that the server already performs and weights each edge by its transfer type. It computes how many times the residual at each holder will be copied and selects the cheapest set of holders whose correction bounds the cumulative residual after the request. A transfer guard and a rejoin rule cover the holders left uncorrected or offline. We prove that partial correction suffices only when the copy number of the lineage graph is below one, that averaging alone never reaches one, and that the correction set remains valid under link outages. On TOFU, HERD leaves 18% to 52% less cumulative residual than the strongest baseline at 6% to 12% of its correction cost.

Purpose Grounded in the Social Information Processing Theory (SIPT), the current study aims to examine the role of Diversity-focused HR Practices in promoting Inclusion Climate; simultaneously, it also investigates the role of Inclusive Leadership as a moderator in relationship explaining how it shapes inclusion at work. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional quantitative approach has been taken, and the survey data were collected from 232 professionals employed in Indian IT sector organizations. To perform the data analysis PLS-SEM was employed using SmartPLS4.1.0 software. Findings The findings reveal while diversity-focused HR practices contribute to fostering an inclusive climate, their impact depends significantly on leadership behavior. Inclusive leaders play a critical role in strengthening the effectiveness of these practices by shaping how employees experience inclusion in their teams. Practical implications The findings of the study imply the gravity that a leader holds in the workgroup. As exhibited by findings, leaders with their inclusive behavior act as a catalyst which transforms HR practices into an inclusive workplace. Therefore, investments in diversity policies must be accompanied by leadership development programs to convert formal initiatives into employees-lived workplace experience. Originality/value The study integrates HR practices and leadership perspectives by identifying inclusive leadership as a contextual boundary condition explaining variability in inclusion climate formation. This shifts scholarly attention from formal HR systems to the role of leaders as enablers of inclusion, demonstrating that leadership is a key mechanism through which diversity initiatives translate into meaningful workplace experiences, thereby providing a novel insight to the present literature.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has complicated writing assignments in college science courses by making it easier for students to produce polished explanations without necessarily engaging deeply with course concepts. Rather than focusing only on preventing or detecting AI use, instructors need assignments that preserve the work of student thinking when AI is readily available. This article describes “A Letter from the HMS Beagle,” a low-stakes assignment used in a large introductory Biology II course. Students imagined themselves as traveling companions of Charles Darwin and wrote a one-page, handwritten letter explaining natural selection through scientific evidence and a historically framed narrative. AI use was permitted during preparation, but the final response had to be handwritten on a provided sheet and submitted in person. The assignment combined scientific explanation, evidence use, historical imagination, and a deliberate procedural constraint. Rather than attempting to make student writing AI-proof, the design emphasized explanation, interpretation, and personal engagement. The activity offers a practical model for preserving scientific thinking and student engagement in AI-mediated science classrooms.

This study maps the importance, perceived needs, and competency gap of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) across four domains—Technical, Strategic, Ethical, Adaptive—and examines their associations with trust, adoption maturity, and industry context. Data were collected from 389 industry professionals in Indonesia using purposive and snowball sampling. The analysis employed descriptive statistics, Spearman correlation, Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and post-hoc Mann-Whitney U tests. The results indicate relatively high perceived GenAI competency needs across all domains, with the largest perceived gaps in the Technical and Strategic domains. Trust in GenAI was positively associated with perceived competency needs across all four domains and with perceived competency gaps in the Technical, Strategic, and Adaptive domains, but not the Ethical domain. Adoption maturity was associated with differences in several dimensions of industry perceptions, particularly industry-perceived graduate readiness to adopt GenAI and perceived needs in the Adaptive and Strategic domains. Sectoral differences were limited, with significant variation observed only in industry-perceived graduate readiness. The study contributes an integrated perspective linking trust and adoption maturity with perceived GenAI competency needs and gaps in Indonesia, highlighting curricular areas that warrant greater attention to applied Technical and Strategic capabilities across organizational GenAI adoption stages.
